title: Nighttime bathroom trips could reveal hidden health issues — here's when to worry
summary: Nocturia affects half of adults over 50, but experts say frequent nighttime urination could signal sleep apnea, diabetes or an enlarged prostate.
story: Dr. Wendy Troxel shares why getting the recommended amount of nightly shuteye doesn't always leave people refreshed, and outlines the most common reasons for poor sleep quality.
Getting out of bed once during the night to use the bathroom is common, but repeated trips could signal underlying issues, health experts warn.

Waking up more than once a night to urinate can meet the clinical definition of nocturia, which affects about half of adults over 50 and becomes more common with age, according to a recent StudyFinds report. The International Continence Society’s formal definition of nocturia includes even one nighttime trip, but frequency, disruption and a change from a person’s usual pattern all matter.

"Everyone has a baseline of what’s normal urinary frequency for them," Dr. Ali Dabaja, a urologist at Henry Ford Health in Michigan, told the outlet. "But if you wake at least twice to go to the bathroom during eight hours of sleep, that’s considered nocturia."
DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID
Nocturia isn't simply a bladder issue, according to Dr. Jeffrey Chester, a licensed physician and medical director of The Ohana Luxury Addiction Treatment Center in Hawaii.

"A change in nighttime urinary patterns is definitely worth mentioning to a physician or healthcare provider, especially when it begins suddenly, becomes more frequent, or disrupts a person's sleep," Chester told Fox News Digital.
Nighttime bathroom trips can disrupt sleep and may become more common with age. (iStock)
Alcohol and caffeine intake, the amount and timing of fluid consumption, and certain medications can all contribute, he added.
Waking up once isn't a cause for concern, agreed Catherine Darley, a naturopathic doctor and founder of Skilled Sleeper in Seattle.
JUST 10 MINUTES OF DAILY FLOOR EXERCISES MAY IMPROVE BALANCE AND AGILITY, STUDY FINDS
But more than once can be "concerning," she told Fox News Digital.

Experts note that it can raise the risk of falls, especially for those with mobility or balance challenges. Research shows two or more nightly trips to the bathroom are linked to a higher risk of fall-related injuries, StudyFinds reported.
Repeated nighttime wake-ups to use the bathroom can increase fall risks, research has found. (iStock)
Sleep disorders can also be a factor, Darley said, including obstructive sleep apnea, which can affect hormones involved in suppressing urine production overnight.
Restless legs syndrome could also contribute to nighttime urination and is more common with age, Darley added.
OLDER ADULTS TAKING 5 OR MORE PRESCRIPTION DRUGS FACE HIGHER RISK OF DEATH, STUDY FINDS
She advised starting with your primary care provider to look for an underlying cause, and checking in with doctors and pharmacists to see if medications could be involved in frequent bathroom trips.
In some cases, they could adjust the timing to prevent late-night wake-ups.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Other issues could be the cause, too, according to StudyFinds, including diabetes, an overactive bladder, an enlarged prostate and fluid buildup.
Experts say the timing and amount of fluids, caffeine, alcohol and some medications can contribute to nighttime urination. (iStock)
For some people, simple habits can help, including not drinking for roughly two hours before bedtime and stopping alcohol about three hours before bed, Darley said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

She also suggested keeping floors clear of rugs and clutter, using gentle amber lighting, sitting on the edge of the bed before standing to avoid getting dizzy — and installing grab bars for extra support.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Political fights can rip couples apart — therapist shares 3 ways to save a relationship
summary: A marriage therapist reveals three strategies for couples navigating the political divide, from setting boundaries to finding compromise.
story: Dr. Anna Elton discusses why partisan disagreements can create tension between partners, and offers strategies for setting boundaries, staying curious and reconnecting after heated conversations.
More than one-third of Americans report having ended a relationship over political differences, according to recent research – and experts say those divisions may also be straining some marriages.

Some high-profile couples, including Democratic strategist James Carville and his wife, Republican political consultant Mary Matalin, have remained together despite their differing views – but experts say navigating those differences isn't always easy.
Anna Elton, Ph.D., a licensed marriage and family therapist and clinical sexologist in Massachusetts, said she has counseled couples on different sides of the political aisle.
'QUIET QUITTING' COULD SILENTLY DESTROY YOUR MARRIAGE – 4 WAYS TO BRING THE SPARK BACK
"A lot of couples come in and they want to work on communication, and politics can come up in our sessions," Elton, author of "The Formula of Desire," told Fox News Digital.
"I work with a number of couples who are in this place where they have a family, they have kids, but they can't talk about politics."
More than one-third of Americans report having ended a relationship over political differences, according to recent research. (iStock)
For many singles, Elton said, political compatibility is now something they consider early in the dating process.
WHY COUPLES SHOULD FLIRT WITH EACH OTHER EVERY DAY – PLUS THE 'RED FLAG' TO AVOID
She referenced a recent study that found younger adults tend to make assumptions about religion, gender roles, empathy and other characteristics based on political affiliation.
"So, before you get to know the person, you’ve already created this assumption of who this person is."
Younger daters are more likely to choose who they want to date based on political affiliation, experts say. (iStock)

"I've definitely been hearing from my younger clients who are saying, ‘I want to know which political party this person belongs to, and then I'll see if I want to even be going on a date and wasting my time with this person.’"
COMMON MARRIAGE HABIT COULD QUIETLY KILL YOUR SEX LIFE, EXPERT WARNS
For couples who have been married for decades, today's political divisions may present challenges that didn't exist when their relationships began, Elton noted.
The expert offered the following three tips for navigating politically charged conversations with a partner in a healthy way.
No. 1: Set boundaries ahead of time
Come up with rules for the conversation and set the tone before it starts, Elton suggested, noting that the first three minutes of a discussion typically predict the outcome.
Conversations that begin with a harsh tone or accusatory language are unlikely to be productive, she said. "So, before you talk, say, ‘OK, these are our boundaries for this conversation.’"
The first three minutes of a discussion can typically predict the outcome, according to the expert. (iStock)
Those boundaries can also extend to media habits, Elton said, including limiting how much political content couples consume, especially on social media.

"You read certain things and then all of a sudden, you keep scrolling on your social media and you see similar content coming up over and over and over again," Elton said. "And at this point, it creates an illusionary effect."
HOW OFTEN ARE MARRIED PEOPLE HAVING SEX? WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT THE INTIMACY STANDARD IN AMERICA

Hearing the same information repeatedly may lead people to gradually accept it as true, according to Elton. "Now think about two people who are in their echo chambers, and they're exposed to certain information that is contradicting each other."

As a general rule, Elton said couples should be mindful not to spend more time on their phones than they do engaging with each other. Excessive screen time can reduce face-to-face connection, leaving less room for eye contact, conversation and other shared experiences.
Set boundaries regarding how much political content you consume, especially when with your partner, the expert advised. (iStock)
Also, when someone is constantly consuming political content, it can become the primary topic they want to discuss, creating tension when partners hold different views, she cautioned.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

To help reduce conflict, Elton recommended limiting when political news or posts are consumed. She also suggested setting aside one phone-free date night each week to encourage face-to-face connection.
No. 2: Agree to disagree
While couples with differing political views are unlikely to agree on every issue, "agreeing to disagree" can help prevent hostility.
"We can still love each other," Elton said. "It's not going to affect our relationship."

"As soon as it gets to the point of seeing your partner through the lens of ‘if you believe this, this is who you are, and I can’t believe that I'm still in a relationship with you,’ that becomes a problem."
When political beliefs become the defining feature of a partner, relationships can suffer, according to the expert. (iStock)

Elton urged couples not to take political disagreements personally and instead approach them with curiosity. She also recommended looking at the same information together, allowing each partner to ask questions and draw their own conclusions rather than jumping into a heated debate.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The therapist also encouraged couples to focus on areas of common ground rather than viewing disagreements in black-and-white terms.
After a disagreement or failure to compromise, it’s important to always reconnect with your partner, she emphasized.
Never end a fight without re-connecting, the therapist advised. (iStock)
Sharing reassuring words like "I love you" and "You matter to me more than anything else" can be helpful, she said.
"I feel like you always need to say, ‘Hey, I hear what you're saying, but I'm not agreeing, and that's OK.’"
3. Consider the wider impact
When politics come into play in a relationship, it can have an impact on more than just the couple.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Elton encouraged partners to consider how sharing certain opinions can impact other loved ones, especially if one person confides in a family member or friend about the other's views.
"You can create this triangulation where you're connecting with someone against your partner, and you don't want that," she warned.

"Talk to your therapist, vent to your therapist… because if you start venting to your family and friends, then they start forming certain opinions about your partner, and it can affect how they talk to them, how they interact with them."
Before making any drastic decisions, such as ending a relationship over political discord, Elton suggested slowing down and returning to a more grounded state.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"We hear certain things and we fill in the gaps," she said. "When we hear someone's political affiliation, we often make assumptions about who they are without really hearing them out."
Rather than making assumptions based on the media or podcasts a partner consumes, for example, Elton encouraged couples to ask questions, stay curious and remain open-minded.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 'Very hot' coffee and tea linked to higher cancer risk in nearly 1 million adults
summary: A University of Oxford study of nearly 1 million adults links very hot tea and coffee to a threefold higher risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
story: Dr. Aaron Sasson, chief of surgical oncology at Stony Brook Cancer Center in New York, confirmed that drinking hot beverages or drinking hot liquids can irritate the esophagus, which could contribute to the development of esophageal cancer.
Regularly drinking very hot tea or coffee may raise the risk of a type of esophageal cancer, according to a large study at the University of Oxford.

People who reported drinking beverages "very hot" had about three times the risk of developing oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), a type of cancer that begins in the cells lining the esophagus, compared to those who drank warm beverages.

Drinking six or more hot drinks per day was associated with a 71% higher risk of the disease. The same link was not seen for esophageal adenocarcinoma (AC), a type of cancer that develops in the lower part of the esophagus.
ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND

The study included nearly 1 million U.K. adults, making it the largest investigation of its kind to date, according to lead study author Keren Papier, a nutritional epidemiologist at the University of Oxford.

Roughly half of the participants were from the Million Women Study (MWS), who were followed for an average of 14 years, and the other half were from the UK Biobank (UKB), who were followed for 11 years.
Regularly drinking very hot tea or coffee may raise the risk of a type of esophageal cancer, according to a large study at the University of Oxford. (iStock)

"Compared with people who reported drinking their beverages ‘warm,’ those who drank them ‘hot’ had around a 1.7 times higher risk of SCC, while those who drank them ‘very hot’ had around a three times higher risk," Papier told Fox News Digital.
The study was published in the International Journal of Cancer.
FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE

The researchers estimated that, if the observed association reflects a true cause-and-effect relationship, about 14% of SCC cases could potentially be prevented if people drank beverages "hot" rather than "very hot."

The biggest limitation, according to the researchers, is that beverage temperatures were self-reported rather than directly measured. Because people's tolerance for heat differs, participants may have classified similar temperatures differently.
"If you are a heavy consumer of hot tea or coffee, maybe you'd want to cool it down a little bit."

"A limitation of our study was that, although we examined associations by self-reported preferred drink temperature, we did not have data on directly measured drink temperatures, and, therefore, cannot determine how self-reported drink temperature is likely to relate to absolute drink temperature," Papier noted.
"These findings don't mean people need to stop drinking tea or coffee. Just let your drinks cool down a little before drinking them."

People who reported drinking beverages "very hot" had about three times the risk of developing oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, a type of cancer that begins in the cells lining the esophagus, compared to those who drank warm beverages. (iStock)
An outside cancer specialist agreed the findings are biologically plausible but said they should be interpreted in context.

Dr. Aaron Sasson, chief of surgical oncology and co-director of the gastrointestinal oncology team at Stony Brook Cancer Center in New York, said it’s been known that drinking hot beverages or liquids can be irritating to the esophagus and that it could contribute to the development of esophageal cancer.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The hotter the liquid, the higher the risk of a "thermal injury," the doctor told Fox News Digital.

"Similar to burning your hand, if you were to get a burn on your hand, you have an increased risk of getting squamous cell carcinoma of the hand, of the skin developing in the burned area," Sasson said. "So, think of that as constantly repeating a burn to the esophagus."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The doctor reiterated that this study specifically looked at the risk of squamous carcinomas, not adenocarcinomas.
"In the United States, about 85% of all of our cancers are adenocarcinomas. So, the incidence of squamous carcinomas in the esophagus is quite low, just to put it into perspective," he noted.
The hotter the liquid, the higher the risk of a "thermal injury," a doctor told Fox News Digital. (iStock)
The lifetime risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus in the U.S. is less than 1%, the doctor said.
Sasson agreed that there was no "objective measurement" of the drinks’ temperature, which poses an unknown variable.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"If you are a heavy consumer of hot tea or coffee, maybe you'd want to cool it down a little bit," he advised. "But I think, for practical purposes, for most people, [it’s] not the predominant risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Smoking, heavy alcohol use, acid reflux and obesity are among the better-established risk factors for esophageal cancer, Sasson said.
"If you were to limit alcohol consumption and eliminate cigarette smoking, you will have done wonders for your esophagus."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Son who lost father in 9/11 attacks shares powerful lessons 25 years later: ‘I’m still here’
summary: A 9/11 survivor's son reveals the grief techniques that transformed his mental health 25 years after losing his father at the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.
story: Grief podcaster David Ferrugio, author of "You’re Not Dead Yet," reflects on losing his dad in the Sept. 11 attacks and why hearing others’ experiences has reshaped his outlook.
As the nation marks 25 years since Sept. 11, 2001, the weight of the loss of loved ones still looms.
Podcaster David Ferrugio, author of the new book "You're Not Dead Yet," joined Fox News Digital to discuss how his own grief persists 25 years after 9/11.
The host of the "DEAD Talks" podcast lost his father, David Frances Ferrugio, who worked at the World Trade Center, in the 9/11 terrorist attacks.
GROUND ZERO FIRST RESPONDER NEEDED MAJOR SURGERY DECADES AFTER 9/11 EXPOSURE: 'I THOUGHT IT WAS OVER'
Ferrugio, who was 12 years old and living in New Jersey at the time, recalls watching television footage of the towers collapsing and "breaking down."

"It was like a dividing moment in my memory and my life, because I was one person on September 11th, and then on September 12th, it was a whole new reality I walked into, which inspired what I'm doing."
Podcaster David Ferrugio lost his father in the 9/11 attacks when he was 12 years old. (David Ferrugio)
After years of internalizing his emotions, Ferrugio discovered the power of sharing stories of grief.
On his podcast, he invites guests to discuss their own experiences with death and loss.
MAN TURNS TRAGIC LOSS OF BEST FRIEND TO SUICIDE INTO URGENT OUTREACH TO LONELY STRANGERS
"Eventually, I got comfortable expressing myself and learning the importance of just sharing [my] story and telling people how I feel and opening up," he said.
Drawing from his own experiences, Ferrugio shares several lessons that have helped him navigate grief.
No. 1: Embrace the uncomfortable

Although discussions of grief can be difficult, even decades after a traumatic event like 9/11, Ferrugio said "embracing the uncomfortable" and talking it out is "an important piece of this complex puzzle."
Sharing stories of loss can provide emotional release while also helping others feel less alone, he noted, adding that he's seen firsthand how those conversations can make a difference.
According to Ferrugio, it’s important to allow for moments of joy, even during times of grief. (David Ferrugio)
"Even when I have my days of just not feeling it, I'm reminded by the people who reach out and the way they share their story ... how much it is impacting so many people."
Finding a sense of community can be especially meaningful at a time when so many people are experiencing loneliness, whether they're grieving or not, Ferrugio added.
FAITH CAN BRING HEALING 25 YEARS AFTER SEPTEMBER 11 TRAGEDY, PASTOR SAYS
"I've learned so much through the eyes of others, and I think the storytelling is just so vital."
Fear of judgment often keeps people from sharing their stories, even though doing so can bring a sense of "liberation," according to Ferrugio.
As the nation marks 25 years since Sept. 11, 2001, the loss of loved ones still weighs heavily.  (iStock)
No. 2: Embrace a new perspective
More than two decades after the attacks, Ferrugio shared that his mental health has improved after putting in "a lot of effort," including shifting his perspective on life and death.
"Life and death are the same coin, just two different sides – and there's a thin veil between them," he said.

"It’s completely shifted the way I live my life through seeing what other people are going through ... understanding the pain people are experiencing, how they manage it ... how they reframe it, and understanding that as alone as this life can feel, we're not as alone as we think."
"It's important to zoom out and realize, ‘I've done this for 25 years, and I'm still here.'"
Grief can reshape how people approach life, Ferrugio said, encouraging them to be more present, embrace the full range of emotions and give themselves grace, even during life's most difficult times.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Ultimately, all these conversations I've had are conversations about grief, but they're really conversations about how we can live this life."
No. 3: Breathe
When painful emotions or a wave of grief start to roll in, Ferrugio's go-to technique is to allow himself to feel it and "breathe it out."
"A lot of breath work works wonders for me," he said. "A deep breath is going to do more for you than you think."
Along with breath work, Ferrugio said exercising and spending time in nature have helped calm his nervous system, noting that what works best varies from person to person.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"We forget to look inward, and we all have that intuition and that guttural feeling – we have to trust what we're saying to ourselves," he said. "What feels good? Does this feel like it's working?"
No. 4: Find light in the dark
It’s important to allow for moments of joy, even during times of grief, said Ferrugio.

"Give yourself permission to feel moments of levity, to feel moments of joy, even if it is for five seconds. … Just take those moments and cherish them, because the contrast of the joy and pain exists for a reason."
Two flags flutter on a fence in front of Lower Manhattan and One World Trade Center at the Tear Drop 9/11 Memorial at sunset on June 13, 2026, in Bayonne, New Jersey. (Gary Hershorn/Getty Images)

"It's not easy to feel however you feel, but it takes a lot of effort and discomfort to try to step out of that. … Whatever we go through in life, it's an ebb and flow, and sometimes both are happening at the same time."
On the 25th anniversary of 9/11, Ferrugio acknowledged that the pain of losing his father remains.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"For anyone else who's been part of that day, I just hope they look back at the days they've gone through and see that they're still here," he said.
"You're still with us, and you’re still grinding. You're showing up for the people in your life."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"It's important to zoom out and realize, ‘I've done this for 25 years, and I'm still here.’"
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Alcohol tied to surprising cancer death pattern in adults under 55, researchers find
summary: Alcohol-attributable cancer deaths in the United States more than doubled from 1990 to 2023, with colorectal cancer surpassing liver cancer in younger men.
story: A University of Miami cancer expert reveals why alcohol is an increasingly important modifiable cancer risk factor, including its potential role in colorectal cancer among younger men.

Annual U.S. cancer deaths tied to alcohol consumption more than doubled over a three-decade period, according to a recent study led by researchers at the Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine.

The findings, published in The Lancet Regional Health — Americas and presented at the American Society of Clinical Oncology Annual Meeting in Chicago, revealed that alcohol-attributable cancer deaths jumped from 11,361 in 1990 to 23,126 in 2023.
Researchers analyzed more than 30 years of data from the Global Burden of Disease study to track the trends.
BEER, WINE OR LIQUOR? MASSIVE STUDY REVEALS WHICH WAS LINKED TO LOWER DEATH RISK
While alcohol has long been classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, surveys show that awareness of its link to cancer remains limited.

"The most surprising finding was the breadth of alcohol’s potential impact across cancer types," Chinmay Jani, M.D., corresponding author of the study and chief fellow in hematology and oncology at Sylvester, told Fox News Digital.
The study highlights that liquor may have a different risk profile than wine despite containing similar amounts of alcohol. (iStock)

"Although its relationship with liver cancer is widely recognized, its contribution to cancers such as colorectal, esophageal, breast, pancreatic and prostate cancer is less understood by the public."
CANCER DOCTOR REVEALS 5 HABITS THAT MAY REDUCE DISEASE RISK AND IMPROVE OUTCOMES

The research showed that older adults and men bore the highest overall burden of alcohol-related cancer deaths. Among older men, liver cancer was the primary cause of alcohol-attributable mortality, followed closely by esophageal and colorectal cancers.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Breast cancer was the leading cause of alcohol-related cancer deaths among women overall, the study found.

Among younger adults between the ages of 20 and 54, colorectal cancer emerged as the leading cause of alcohol-attributable cancer deaths in men and the second leading cause in women, surpassing liver cancer in both groups.
Breast cancer was the leading cause of alcohol-related cancer deaths among women overall, the study found. (iStock)

The authors noted that the findings carry significant weight for public health messaging, particularly because general awareness surrounding alcohol's connection to various cancers remains low compared to known risks like tobacco use.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Because no minimum "safe" level of alcohol has been established, researchers said drinking less may help lower long-term cancer risk.
Because the study used existing national data rather than following individuals over time, researchers couldn’t determine each person’s exact drinking habits or account for every lifestyle factor.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

As a result, the findings show a strong association between alcohol use and cancer deaths, but they cannot prove that alcohol directly caused those deaths or establish a specific "safe" drinking limit.
The findings show a strong association between alcohol use and cancer deaths, but they cannot prove that alcohol directly caused those deaths or establish a specific "safe" drinking limit. (iStock)

"What this study makes clear is that alcohol-related cancer risk is not limited to one disease or one group of people," Gilberto Lopes, M.D., senior author and chief of the Division of Medical Oncology at the Miller School, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"As physicians and cancer researchers, we have an opportunity to help patients understand that alcohol is a modifiable risk factor and that even small, informed changes can be part of a broader strategy to reduce cancer risk in our community."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Ground Zero first responder needed major surgery decades after 9/11 exposure: ‘I thought it was over’
summary: Volunteer EMT Mordechai Shedrowitzky shares how Ground Zero dust exposure led to years of hospitalizations, steroids and a rare airway disease diagnosis.
story: Volunteer EMT Mordechai Shedrowitzky and an NYU doctor share how exposure to World Trade Center dust can have serious health consequences decades later.
Those who were present at Ground Zero on Sept. 11, 2001, continue to experience the physical effects of their exposure.
As Lower Manhattan was engulfed in dust and debris from the remnants of both towers, first responders and survivors were forced to breathe in toxic air.

More than 400,000 people were exposed to toxic contaminants, physical-injury risks and stressful conditions in the days, weeks and months following the attacks, according to the World Trade Center Health Program.
SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POSSIBLE LINK BETWEEN 9/11 AND ACCELERATED AGING

As of March 2025, 8,215 people who had enrolled in the WTC Health Program had died, including 5,844 responders, as reported by the CDC. The figures include deaths from all causes; the program does not track whether a member’s death was related to 9/11 exposure.
A responder’s long-term health battle
In an interview with Fox News Digital, Mordechai Shedrowitzky, a volunteer EMT who responded on 9/11, shared how his exposure led to multiple hospitalizations and, ultimately, major surgery.

FDNY firefighters and rescue workers attend to an injured firefighter in the rubble of the World Trade Center in Manhattan, New York, after it was destroyed by planes in a terrorist attack on Sept. 11, 2001. (Getty Images)

Queens-born Shedrowitzky, 51, was living in Brooklyn at the time of the attacks. After helping cover his local area for much of the day, he headed into Lower Manhattan that evening to assist with the response.

"My most vivid memory was actually entering Manhattan from Brooklyn," he said. "As we approached the tunnel, the first thing we noticed was there were no lights, there was no electricity in the area, it [was] pitch black."
FOX NEWS' ERIC SHAWN REVEALS CANCER AND RESPIRATORY ILLNESS FROM 9/11 TOXIC DUST
"When we entered the tunnel, there was a tremendous amount of swirling debris, at speeds that I just can't even imagine."
Once Shedrowitzky and his team arrived at South Street Seaport, where his ambulance was staged with others, he described the debris as "overwhelming."
"I remember the engine actually sputtering at times," he said. "I would imagine that it was taking in a tremendous amount of dust."
Firefighters gather near ground zero after the attack on the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001. (Corbis via Getty Images)

"We were definitely not cognizant of what effect ... the air might have on us. And therefore, we did spend a significant amount of time outside of the ambulances, just commiserating with the people around us."
Shedrowitzky said he "thought it was over" once he left the scene. But years later, he noticed small symptoms that were turning into a big problem.
His pre-existing asthma — which typically flared during seasonal changes and caused coughing that required an inhaler — was worsening each year.
AMERICA'S FIREFIGHTER SHORTAGE HITS CRISIS LEVEL AS EMERGENCY CALLS TRIPLE, PUTTING LIVES AT RISK

"I started to require oral steroids," he said. "I would have wheezing; I would have coughing. It would last longer; it would be more serious ... I wouldn't be able to go to work, wouldn’t be able to take care of my kids. So, the effects were definitely increasing over time."
Shedrowitzky added that his condition was "getting to the point where it was leading to frequent respiratory infections and hospitalizations."
A graphic shows a close-up of dust particles breathed in during the 9/11 terrorist attacks. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
"It took a number of years, many years, for us to realize that what was going on with my health was probably related to 9/11."
In 2019, Shedrowitzky described that his condition got "significantly worse," after experiencing a cough that wouldn’t resolve itself, even after the "highest doses" of steroids and antibiotics.
NAVY VETERANS REUNITE AFTER 30 YEARS FOR 'GRUELING' CROSS-COUNTRY BIKE CHALLENGE HONORING 9/11
Shedrowitzky ultimately was put in touch with the World Trade Center Health Program – a federal program administered by the CDC – where his condition was classified as 9/11-related and was monitored.
It was eventually confirmed that Shedrowitzky had tracheobronchomalacia, a condition in which the walls of the windpipe and major airways weaken and collapse during breathing.
Mordechai Shedrowitzky and Dr. Denise Harrison of NYU Langone's WTC Health Program are pictured on Sept. 8, 2026. (Khloe Quill/Fox News Digital)
"[It] was probably secondary to both the asthma getting worse as well as steroid use over the years to try to treat those symptoms," he said.
In 2024, Shedrowitzky underwent a procedure called a tracheobronchoplasty to structurally reinforce his trachea and main bronchi.
RUDY GIULIANI REVEALS HE HAD 'SPIRITUAL EXPERIENCE' WHILE IN PNEUMONIA-RELATED COMA
Two years after the procedure, he said he is feeling "much better," although he still experiences occasional infections. He hopes to return to work as a physical therapist soon.
"Even a couple of months ago, I wouldn't have been able to speak for more than a very short time," Shedrowitzky said.
"It took a number of years, many years, for us to realize that what was going on with my health was probably related to 9/11."
As a father of six, Shedrowitzky – who is now also a grandfather of two – said his condition made it difficult for him to spend time with his children as they were growing up.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Things as simple as lifting my children, even speaking to them," he said. "The amount of time that I spent in the hospital and its effect on them was quite significant."
"Now, they're older, but my ability to spend time, interact with them ... has been greatly improved."
Treating 9/11-related illnesses
Dr. Denise Harrison, medical director of the NYU Grossman School of Medicine WTC Health Program Clinical Center of Excellence, has been involved in post-9/11 healthcare since 2002.
The program has since grown to provide screening, monitoring and treatment for people experiencing health effects related to their 9/11 exposure.
The doctor noted that the dust on 9/11 was "highly alkaline," which can be "very irritating" to the airways.
People rush away from the collapsing World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001, after two hijacked airplanes hit the twin towers in New York City in a terrorist attack. (Getty Images)

"Usually, the larger size dust gets deposited in the upper airways and the smaller size dust gets deposited in the lower airways," she told Fox News Digital. "Because of the overwhelming nature of the disaster, a significant number of large particles got deposited into the lower airways as well. So, this is not just the airways, but also the digestive tract, in the esophagus."

Harrison said patients often report sinus problems, asthma and COPD. These conditions can occur alongside other "aerodigestive" issues, including gastroesophageal reflux disease, which may complicate diagnosis and treatment.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Other 9/11-related conditions may also be interlinked.
"We have patients with asthma and PTSD who might perceive their asthma symptoms differently than the patients without PTSD, so that requires a combination of providers," the doctor said.
The dust on 9/11 was "highly alkaline," which can be "very irritating" to the airways, the doctor noted. (iStock)
Shedrowitzky urged other first responders who are experiencing health issues to not wait to get help and to confirm that what they’re experiencing may be linked to 9/11.
"Continue to be monitored so that potential issues can be picked up early," he advised.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"If we can look back and see the quality of life that it's robbing you of, it might push you to contact the World Trade Center Health Program, get the help that you need."
NYU Langone's WTC Health Program 9/11 exhibit is on display. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
As of March 31, 2025, the WTC Health Program had more than 130,000 currently enrolled members.
The program, which is authorized through 2090, operates branches across multiple health systems, including NYU Langone Health, Mount Sinai, Northwell, Stony Brook and Rutgers.

Harrison reiterated that the health effects of 9/11 exposure remain "persistent," and can be exacerbated by the environment and other illnesses. Experts predict that the fallout will continue for decades to come.

"Symptoms are still ongoing and research is still ongoing," she said, urging the public and responders to "have patience."
"While it might not directly benefit them or may provide some benefits now, it could be more beneficial in the future and help the overall response to disasters."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Reporter's Notebook: House control could hinge on whether the old political rules still apply
summary: Trump's mid-30s approval and high gas prices favor Democrats, but redistricting and turnout questions could keep House races razor-tight.
story: Congress faces a critical decision on the future of artificial intelligence as lawmakers debate potential regulations on Capitol Hill. Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the bipartisan push for guidelines.
Are we playing with the old playbook or a new playbook in the midterm elections this fall?
That’s unclear. It’s hard to determine, simply because we’ve seen so much that’s "new" in politics lately.

Norms are cast aside. The American system quaked to its core in recent years. You’ve witnessed an American president win the election by prevailing in the Electoral College but losing the popular vote. To have that happen twice in 16 years (2000 and 2016) is astonishing, considering the fact that such an outcome only unfolded on three occasions before.
You then had a president impeached twice – yet return to office a few years later. There was the Capitol riot, as arguing continued about the 2020 election.
FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS WANT MAJOR CHANGE AMID ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL DISCONTENT

President Donald Trump arrives to host a dinner in the Rose Garden of the White House on Sept. 2, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Trump invited Republicans running in competitive races ahead of the November elections. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

If this is the old playbook, Democrats likely light up the scoreboard in November. The party of the President typically loses about 25 seats in a president’s first midterm. Midterm elections are frequently a referendum on the President. That’s why many Republicans are trying to keep President Donald Trump at arm’s length, considering that his polling numbers are anywhere from the mid-thirties to 40 percent on a good day. Gas prices are high. Grocery prices are skyrocketing. The war in Iran lingers. There’s a trade war with one of America’s best allies.
On the old playbook, this portends a disaster for the GOP in this fall’s midterms.
But what if we’re using the new playbook?

President Trump – and sometimes Republicans aligned with him – have shown a remarkable resilience to defy political gravity and norms. Control of the House could come down to just a few seats. What if there are questions about election security and the validity of who won and lost? There’s redistricting. On paper, Republicans probably redrew about five to six seats nationwide in their favor.
If things are tight, we might not know which party wins the House on election night. Perhaps a few days down the road – if not later. That is, unless it’s a Democratic blowout.

And, remember what we said a few moments ago about the president’s party losing so many seats in that first midterm? Yes, in a way, this is President Trump’s "first midterm." But not really. He experienced a midterm in 2018. Not that things went in the GOP’s favor that year. There’s no contemporary data on how the party of a President might perform after he’s been out of office and rallied to victory a few years later.

Also, the sheer reduction by both parties of seats which are in play mitigates political "waves" which crash across the political shoreline in House midterm races. Think 1994 and 2010 for Republicans. 2018 for Democrats.Thus, even though many of the factors favor the Democrats, the possibility remains it could be tough for the party to flip the House.

In 2018, the Democrats’ carried an approval rating of 44%. For this time around, it’s 37%. That rivals polling related to the President. In 2018, voters had had enough of President Trump and wanted a change. But because of the polling parity this year, it’s not so obvious that voters are so turned off by President Trump that they automatically gravitate to the Democrats.
Here’s another factor: turnout.
FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: WHAT’S IN AN ECONOMY?
The sun sets behind the U.S. Capitol Dome on Sept. 4, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

President Trump has worked hard to tell voters that he’s "on the ballot" this fall. That cuts two ways. President Trump’s presence on the ballot has historically driven people to the polls. In 2016, 60.1% of registered voters showed up. In 2020, an eye-popping 66.4% of all voters cast ballots. And in 2024, 64.3% of those registered to vote did so.

But considering the president’s unpopularity, the cognizance of voters that he’s "on the ballot" could also deter them from turning out. At least those who previously supported him. And those impacts ricochet down to House races. The President’s track record at turning out independent voters in races which count wasn’t great down ballot – even as he won the White House in 2024.

Consider that in the 2018 midterms, 50.1% of registered voters materialized. Just 46.1% voted in the 2022 midterms. It was 36.1% in the 2014 midterms — 41% in the historic 2010 midterms where Republicans won a record 63 House seats.

This "Trump on the ballot" initiative might not resound with voters. Especially since the President conceded – en route to his midterm convention in Dallas – that gas prices wouldn’t decrease until after the election. He also said the U.S. is stuck with the war in Iran through the midterms.
So how do we know what to anticipate in November?
It’s really hard to read if there’s not a clear wave coming. The best way to postulate control of the House is by going race to race. And that is a painstaking process.

For instance, will Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, D-Mo., have a district in which to run? Missouri Republicans tried to draw Cleaver out of his district earlier this year. Then a court ruled last week that the Show-Me-State must use the old Congressional districts – likely meaning that Cleaver was safe. Then another judge ruled that voters already cast ballots in primaries. So the new maps were back and Cleaver may be out.
All of this less than two months before the election.
MISSOURI HIGH COURT BLOCKS GOP-BACKED CONGRESSIONAL MAPS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS; TRUMP BLASTS 'RIDICULOUS' RULING
Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol on December 16, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Is there a groundswell for Democrats in Iowa where the Senate seat and governor’s mansion are in jeopardy for Republicans? If that’s the case, Democrats might have a shot of claiming at least two if not three seats there: Republican Iowa Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, Zach Nunn and maybe the seat that Rep. Ashley Hinson is vacating in her quest to become a senator.

How about Ohio? There are competitive gubernatorial and Senate contests. Does a Democratic surge boost Rep. Greg Landsman, D-Ohio? Do the accusations of spousal and child abuse bounce embattled Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio., in what is otherwise a relatively safe Republican seat? Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, clung to her seat by fewer than 1,000 votes two years ago. But that was when President Trump carried the Buckeye State by 11 points – and Kaptur’s district. Redistricting actually turned Kaptur’s turf slightly more in her favor. But the 80-year-old Kaptur was in a car wreck in August, inhibiting her ability to campaign. Is that a factor?

How well do Democrats perform in Virginia? Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Va., faces former Rep. Elaine Luria, D-Va., who she vanquished in 2022. Could former Rep. Tom Perriello, D-Va., – who won in a 2008 upset in a differently-drawn district and promptly lost in 2010 – unseat Rep. John McGuire, R-Va.?

Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, is retiring. Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage (R) is running for Golden’s seat. Does LePage benefit from Democratic chaos in the effort to unseat Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine? After all, President Trump won one of Maine’s three electoral votes in 2024, capturing that Congressional district over former Vice President Kamala Harris.
We could bounce around the map, district to district, all day like this. But sans a wave, that’s what you must do to properly filet the House races.
Most conventional arrows point in the direction of Democrats winning the House this fall. Yet it probably shouldn’t be this close.
That’s why you have to go by the playbook.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The only question is if this is the old playbook or new playbook?
Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: Ex-Dem insider drops bombshell on where Harris ranked in secret poll for Biden replacements
summary: Lindy Li says Democratic internal polling showed Kamala Harris ranked dead last among potential Biden replacements, behind Pete Buttigieg and others.
story: Even so, former Biden-Harris fundraiser Lindy Li claims party leaders feared the fallout from passing over the vice president.

FIRST ON FOX: Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser who switched her party affiliation over unheeded warning signs about President Joe Biden's decline in the 2024 election, says Democrats had internal polling showing that Kamala Harris was far from the party’s best shot at beating Donald Trump.
But that polling wasn’t convenient.
"The polling numbers went directly against the narrative that the party wanted to espouse," Li said.

"They knew that skipping over Kamala Harris would be a slap in the face to the bedrock of the party, which is Black women in particular, and they just wouldn't have it," Li told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.
EX-DEM INSIDER EXPOSES WHAT HARRIS TOLD TOP DONORS DAYS BEFORE BIDEN DROPPED OUT: 'INSULTING'
Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser, left, posing for a picture with former President Joe Biden, right at a 2023 campaign event. (Lindy Li)

Li is chronicling the months leading up to Biden's withdrawal from the race in her new book, "Unburdened," revealing that the party’s internal thinking behind why Harris was made the nominee and how many of the party’s top figures had long known that Biden’s age had created an unavoidable political liability.

Li recalled that former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Harris had been floated as possible replacements for Biden before Biden announced his decision to step down.
According to Li, Harris was at the bottom of the group.

"Kamala Harris came in dead last. It wasn't even close. Pete Buttigieg, who hilariously received 0% support from the Black vote, did better than she did. And yet the party is so straitjacketed by DEI that they had no choice but to appoint her," Li said.

As a top fundraiser for both Biden and Harris, Li worked closely with top donors, high-profile members of the party and the Democratic National Committee (DNC). She recalled how the polling was guarded closely, but that it circulated among the party’s leading operatives and fundraisers like herself.
FORMER DNC FUNDRAISER SAYS MAJOR DONORS WON’T BACK KAMALA HARRIS AGAIN AS PARTY FACES DIVISIONS

Former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris discusses her new memoir '107 Days' at the Southbank Centre's London Literature Festival 2025, in London on Thursday Oct. 23, 2025. (Manning/PA Images via Getty Images)

"I’m part of the National Finance Committee. The list of membership is guarded like the papal conclave. But people talk. It's a very small group of people. That poll was commissioned internally," Li said.

"Most of the time I would say I don't believe a candidate's polling because it's basically just funded propaganda. But in this case we wanted an objective overview of who could actually mount the most formidable opposition to Trump."
At the end of the day, Li believes that the decision to put Harris at the top of the ticket was made, at least partially, out of fear.
In addition to being the vice president and an obvious replacement consideration for Biden, Li recalled that Kamala had devoted followers who would make it painful to explore other options.

"People were terrified of the online mob. The K-Hive isn’t that numerous, but they’re very, very toxic and they’re very coordinated. No one wants to be labeled as a racist," Li said, referring to the nickname for Harris’ supporters.

Li believes that, using that fear and by positioning herself close to Biden’s donors, Harris made herself the choice the party couldn’t turn a blind eye to, despite knowledge of her weakness as a candidate.
HOW TRUMP PANIC BROKE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY AND FUELED ENDLESS CRISIS POLITICS
Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser, pictured alongside former President Joe Biden, right. (Lindy Li; Sean Rayford/Getty Images)
"Oscar-worthy. Honestly, truly Oscar-worthy," Li said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Representatives for Harris did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Russian spies orchestrated $40K murder plot in nation’s capital, US alleges
summary: Five Russian intelligence operatives allegedly offered $40,000 to a U.S.-based recruit to kill a Kremlin critic believed to live in Washington, D.C.
story: Stuart Varney and Victoria Coates discuss allegations that Russia targeted Zelensky's plane with drones. Coates analyzes the security implications of these actions, claiming Putin is seeking a kill shot to install a puppet government in Kiev.
The U.S. accused Russian intelligence operatives of orchestrating a murder-for-hire plot targeting a Kremlin critic believed to be living in Washington, D.C.

In documents unsealed on Tuesday, federal prosecutors claim the conspiracy was part of a broader global network that recruited people to carry out assassinations and terrorist attacks on behalf of Moscow. The five men charged in the incitement allegedly worked for Russia's intelligence services, and are accused of being paid and attempting to pay others in the U.S. and abroad to surveil and kill Russian dissidents.
Three of the defendants also face conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire charges. All five defendants remain at large, according to the Justice Department.
People walk through Red Square near Kremlin towers, St. Basil's Cathedral and the State Historical Museum in Moscow, Russia, September 10, 2026. (Anastasia Barashkova/Reuters)

According to prosecutors, the alleged operation reached the nation's capital in late August, when suspected Russian intelligence operatives directed a U.S.-based Venezuelan citizen to secretly film two Washington-area locations tied to a Kremlin critic before allegedly offering him $40,000 to carry out the killing. The recruit completed the surveillance but refused to commit the murder himself, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors allege the five defendants were members or associates of a Russian intelligence-directed network that financed terrorism and coordinated violent operations across multiple countries.

The recruiter walked the operative through the surveillance step by step, prosecutors say, and allegedly instructed him to put his phone in airplane mode, begin recording before entering the neighborhood, slow as he passed the target's home and delete the messages afterward.

The indictment says the conspirators used coded language, referring to the assassination as "construction" and the surveillance as "measuring a plot of land." When the recruit declined to carry out the murder himself, prosecutors allege the network sought other U.S.-based recruits while noting it also had "people in Mexico" available for the job.
RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT

In addition to the alleged murder plot in Washington, the indictment accuses members of the network of supporting attacks on civilian and military infrastructure in Europe and carrying out surveillance of Russian dissidents abroad.

President Donald Trump walks with Russian President Vladimir Putin as they arrive at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson Aug. 15, 2025, in Anchorage, Alaska. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said today (Friday) Russia has "not received anything officially" from Washington on the 28-point plan. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
The case marks one of the most serious publicly alleged Russian intelligence operations targeting an individual inside the U.S. in recent years.

The indictment names five alleged members of what prosecutors call the Russian Intelligence Services Network (RIS). They include Yuri Khrameev, a former Russian intelligence colonel known as "Colonel Yuri"; his son, Kirill Khrameev, an officer in Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB); Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, a Cuban national living in Russia whom prosecutors describe as coordinating attacks for the network; and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, known as "Viking," and Angel Eduardo Castro.
Russia has repeatedly been accused by Western governments of targeting political opponents and defectors abroad.

Among the highest-profile cases was the 2018 poisoning of former Russian intelligence officer Sergei Skripal and his daughter in Salisbury, England, with the military-grade nerve agent Novichok. British authorities blamed Russian military intelligence for the attack, an allegation Moscow denied.

U.S. officials have also accused Russia of orchestrating killings of Kremlin critics overseas and conducting covert influence and espionage operations inside the United States, though prosecutors say the alleged Washington murder plot represents a rare instance in which Russian operatives sought to recruit someone on U.S. soil to carry out an assassination.
The U.S. Capitol building is seen on August 7, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
RUSSIA UNLEASHES NEARLY 600 MISSILES AND DRONES ON KYIV IN DEADLIEST STRIKE SINCE MAY

Prosecutors say the alleged Washington murder plot was part of a much broader Russian intelligence campaign that has operated since at least 2024. According to the indictment, the same network recruited a U.S. citizen in Lithuania to surveil another Kremlin critic before allegedly offering about $25,000 to kill him.

After that recruit refused, prosecutors say the network shifted to soliciting sabotage attacks against infrastructure in countries supporting Ukraine, including alleged plots targeting electrical substations , warehouses and transportation hubs.

The indictment comes as Western governments have warned that Russia has expanded its use of covert operations, sabotage and assassination plots beyond the battlefield since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
U.S. prosecutors allege the network shifted its focus from targeting Russian dissidents and defectors to attacking countries "aligned, or perceived to be aligned, with Ukraine."

title: White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles announces she is cancer free
summary: The White House chief of staff revealed her pathology results from the Mayo Clinic came back clear, six months after her breast cancer diagnosis.
story: President Trump praised his chief of staff Susie Wiles in a video message presented Thursday, says she will be "in great shape."
White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles announced Wednesday that she is cancer free, six months after revealing she had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer.
"Some personal news I’m grateful to share," Wiles wrote. "After a medical appointment at the Mayo Clinic this week, my pathology results came back clear.

Susie Wiles, White House chief of staff, during an end of summer barbeque with Republican lawmakers in the Rose Garden of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026. (Samuel Corum/Sipa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

title: Tax breaks helping fuel Trump's latest tech push just landed in Dems' crosshairs
summary: House Democrats target bonus depreciation and opportunity zone tax breaks for AI data centers, arguing Big Tech shouldn't get taxpayer subsidies.
story: Rep. Chris Pappas says towns shouldn't have data centers 'shoved down their throats' as Democrats push to block the facilities from tapping key federal tax incentives. (Credit: C-SPAN)
House Democrats are moving to stop data centers from receiving lucrative federal tax breaks as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom accelerates their expansion nationwide.

The moves put Democrats at odds with President Donald Trump as he makes data centers central to his American AI agenda. The administration has sought to accelerate data center development and streamline permitting as the U.S. competes for dominance in the emerging tech industry.
Reps. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., and Don Davis, D-N.C., unveiled legislation Wednesday that would block data centers from tapping certain federal investment incentives.
AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY

Data centers house the computing infrastructure that powers artificial intelligence and other digital services, and demand for the centers is surging across the country. (Ulysse Bellier/AFP/Getty Images)

The incentives in question weren't created specifically for AI or data centers. But the industry's massive infrastructure investments can qualify for these substantial tax benefits, which prompted Democrats to push to exclude data centers as concerns grow over electricity demand, water use and local development.
The bill is backed by 21 additional House Democrats, including Ways and Means Committee member Rep. Jimmy Panetta, D-Calif.
"Washington is giving handouts to Big Tech companies while American families are drowning. I hear that word in my district more than any other," McDonald Rivet said at a news conference Wednesday.

"From rising costs, groceries, gas, housing, healthcare and a lot more. These are backward priorities, and they perfectly encapsulate everything that is wrong with the way Washington works, serving interests of big corporations and special interests at the expense of working people."
THIS TINY FARMING TOWN YOU’VE NEVER HEARD OF IS HELPING MICROSOFT SELL AMERICA ON DATA CENTERS

Data centers are expanding rapidly across the U.S. as companies invest billions in the infrastructure needed to power the artificial intelligence boom. (Mikala Compton/The Austin American-Statesman/Getty Images)

Speaking alongside McDonald Rivet outside the Capitol, Rep. Deborah Ross, D-N.C., pointed to concerns over data center development in her Raleigh-area district, accusing tech companies of buying land without disclosing their plans in a plot to sidestep local input.
"They've sought to bypass local citizens' right to provide input on putting a data center in their towns and cities," Ross said.
The lawmaker also argued that the industry's rapid expansion is straining electricity and water resources while developers benefit from federal and state tax incentives.
"It's Americans struggling to get by, not Big Tech who need tax breaks," Ross said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
President Donald Trump has made the rapid expansion of U.S. data centers a key part of his push to bolster American leadership in artificial intelligence. (Anadolu via Getty Images)
Rep. Chris Pappas, D-N.H., argued that data center development is contributing to higher costs for his constituents as the facilities place growing demands on electricity and water supplies.
He also said communities should have more control over where the facilities are built.
"Our cities and towns shouldn't have these data centers shoved down their throats without any recourse," Pappas said. "They deserve the right to decide what's appropriate for their community."
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Trump surgeon general pick backs MMR vaccine, rejects link between childhood vaccines and autism
summary: Nicole Saphier told senators she does not believe the MMR vaccine is lethal, breaking with Trump's past comments as measles cases surge nationwide.
story: Nicole Saphier, MD, said she does not believe childhood vaccines cause autism and called the MMR vaccine the "greatest tool for combatting measles" during questioning from Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La.

President Donald Trump's latest surgeon general nominee, Dr. Nicole Saphier, defended the MMR vaccine and rejected claims that childhood vaccines cause autism during a Senate confirmation hearing Wednesday.

Saphier, a radiologist and a former Fox News contributor, would serve as the federal government's top doctor and public health spokesperson at a time when measles cases are surging across the country.
"I believe the MMR vaccine is our greatest tool for combatting measles," Saphier said during her appearance before the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions.
Sen. Bill Cassidy, the committee's chairman, asked Saphier whether she agreed with Trump's comments last month suggesting the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine could be "quite lethal."
TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK SPARKS BACKLASH, SPLITS MAHA MOVEMENT

Nicole Saphier, President Donald Trump's nominee for surgeon general, arrives for a Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee confirmation hearing in Washington, D.C. on Sept. 16. 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"As a physician, I can tell you that I do not believe the MMR vaccine to be lethal," Saphier responded.
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who Saphier would serve under if confirmed, has said multiple times throughout his tenure that people should get the MMR vaccine.
"The two-dose MMR vaccine is our safest and most effective tool to prevent this highly contagious illness," he told Fox News Digital in March 2025.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has also continued to recommend the MMR vaccine, although the Trump administration eventually favors splitting it into three shots.

President Donald Trump holds up a signed executive order calling for childhood vaccine shots to be spaced out into separate visits during an event in the Oval Office of the White House on Aug. 10, 2026, in Washington D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
CNN'S DANA BASH SPARS WITH RFK JR OVER VACCINE EFFICACY, DEMANDS HE 'LOOK INTO THE CAMERA' AND PUSH VACCINES
Saphier also differed with some of Kennedy’s past statements about a potential link between vaccines and autism.

"Well, humbly, I don't know what causes autism, but I have not seen reputable evidence that would suggest that vaccines cause autism," Saphier said. "I do not believe childhood vaccines cause autism."
In a 2023 Fox News interview, while running for president as a Democrat, Kennedy told host Jesse Watters: "I do believe that autism does come from vaccines."

Kennedy later backed away from claiming a definitive link between vaccines and autism, saying in his confirmation hearing last year that he would "do nothing as HHS secretary that makes it difficult or discourages people from taking vaccines."

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks during an announcement at the Department of Health and Human Services headquarters in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, July 21, 2026. The Trump administration said it would halt more than $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota after an audit identified instances of fraud. (Tierney L. Cross/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
SENATE CONFIRMS NEW CDC DIRECTOR AS DIARRHEA-CAUSING PARASITE OUTBREAK SWEEPS US
Later, Saphier addressed a question from Cassidy, also a physician, about whether children should receive the hepatitis B vaccine at birth.

"Chairman Cassidy, you're speaking to someone who tells people they have cancer every day. And the hepatitis B vaccine is one of the most tangible ways we have to prevent cancer," she said, adding, "The most tried and true way to prevent hepatitis B infection and effectively lower hepatitis B associated illness is universal birth dosing."

Cassidy repeatedly pressed Saphier on whether she supported the Trump administration's move in December to stop universally recommending the vaccine at birth for babies whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B.
Saphier stopped short of saying whether she believed the policy should be reversed.
Nicole Saphier shakes the hand of Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., ahead of her confirmation hearing to be surgeon general on Sept. 16, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
AMERICAN VACCINES THAT TRANSFORMED PUBLIC HEALTH OVER 250 YEARS: 'OUTWEIGHS HARM'

Under questioning from other senators, Saphier said that as surgeon general, she would promote early cancer screening, review data on the harms of flavored e-cigarettes and study the mental health effects of AI chatbots on children and adolescents.
Saphier was nominated by Trump in April after his earlier pick for surgeon general, wellness influencer Dr. Casey Means, failed to gain enough traction in the Senate to be confirmed.
Before that, Trump withdrew his nomination of Dr. Janette Nesheiwat, another former Fox News contributor, in May 2025.
As the director of breast imaging at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center's location in Monmouth, New Jersey, Saphier would bring extensive medical experience to the role.
Physician and wellness influencer Casey Means speaks at a Senate confirmation hearing on Feb. 26, 2026, when she was the surgeon general nominee. (Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP via Getty Images)
FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS EMBRACE HEALTH AGENDA WHILE RATING RFK JR NEGATIVELY

She has also authored several books on health and wellness, including "Make America Healthy Again: How Bad Behavior and Big Government Caused a Trillion-Dollar Crisis," published in April 2020, mere months after the COVID-19 pandemic began.
Kennedy later adopted the phrase "Make America Healthy Again" as the slogan for his presidential campaign before bringing it into the Trump administration's broader public health agenda.

Before being nominated, Saphier openly criticized Kennedy, writing in a Wall Street Journal op-ed last year that she was "deeply concerned" about his approach after he described autism as an "epidemic" and pledged to identify the cause of the developmental disorder by September 2025.
Nicole Saphier attends the 2025 Fox Nation Patriot Awards at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts on Nov. 6, 2025, in Greenvale, New York. (Roy Rochlin/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Specifically, she took issue with Kennedy hiring David Geier, a vaccine critic, to analyze CDC data on autism. She called his experience "limited" and said his research has been "widely criticized within the scientific and medical communities."
A review of the Health and Human Services employment database shows Geier still works at the department as a "senior data analyst."

"Families deserve more than passionate speeches and fringe science," Saphier wrote in the op-ed. "If Mr. Kennedy truly wants to be a champion for families facing autism spectrum disorder, he should form partnerships with the nation’s most reputable researchers."
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: Fraud expert exposes how hidden networks drove Minnesota fraud, other major scams: 'Criminal enterprise'
summary: Haywood Talcove reveals how criminals use LLCs and stolen identities to bill Medicaid for fake claims, fueling human trafficking and cybercrime.
story: Haywood Talcove, CEO of LexisNexis Risk Solutions Government, told Fox News Digital how fake LLCs, stolen identities and weak oversight helped fuel massive fraud schemes in Minnesota and across the country.

Criminals can turn stolen identities bought on the dark web into seemingly legitimate businesses — then use those companies to bill taxpayers for healthcare and other services that were never provided, according to a fraud expert who detailed the scheme to Fox News Digital.

The companies can hide in plain sight: Criminals create LLCs using information that may receive little scrutiny, pair them with stolen identities and submit fraudulent claims for everything from wheelchairs and diabetes treatments to childcare and autism services, according to Haywood Talcove, CEO of LexisNexis Risk Solutions Government.
But Talcove said the financial losses are only the beginning, warning the schemes can fuel "criminal enterprises."
"They are using our money against us, whether it's in social media campaigns, whether it is for human trafficking, drugs, disrupting our economy," Talcove told Fox News Digital.
STOLEN IDS SOLD FOR ‘HAPPY MEAL’ PRICES FUEL BILLIONS IN US BENEFIT FRAUD

Haywood Talcove, CEO of LexisNexis Risk Solutions, spoke with Fox News Digital about how criminals use fake LLCs and stolen identities to commit fraud. (Elizabeth Flores/Star Tribune via Getty Images ; Fox News Digital)

"When you think about fraud, don't think about, 'It's great that we stopped a fraud ring that stole $5 million.' Think about that as a criminal enterprise that goes beyond just stealing out of a benefit program."
Despite fraud schemes surfacing nationwide, Talcove said Minnesota was "particularly egregious" because the state had little incentive to stop the fraud.
"Minnesota was particularly egregious once they started looking because it was really easy to find," he said.
Talcove said one factor allowing the schemes to flourish in Minnesota and across the country is weak verification during the LLC registration process and reliance on "self-reported information."

"In the case of Minnesota, you went and got your LLC, you opened up a childcare facility, and then the next thing you knew you were billing CMS [Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services] for childcare or autism care, and nobody checked."

The Trump administration launched an anti-fraud crackdown this year after Minnesota's Feeding Our Future scandal, creating a task force led by Vice President JD Vance. The scheme allegedly stole $250 million from a federally funded child nutrition program during the pandemic, and many of those charged have since been convicted or sentenced to prison.
Without third-party audits, Talcove said many criminals slip through the cracks, racking up millions before they're caught.

"One of the fundamental problems with these programs that are literally spending trillions of taxpayer dollars, they have nobody doing investigations or such a small, tiny amount of people that it's not even possible to investigate," he said.
FRAUD EXPERT WARNS AI IS HELPING CRIMINALS OUTPACE THE GOVERNMENT: 'DON'T HAVE THE RIGHT TOOLS'
Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz testifies during a House Oversight and Government Reform Committee hearing at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on March 4, 2026. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
But Talcove said when these schemes are investigated, they expose much more than fraud.
"They're not just involved in stealing Medicare, Medicaid, or food stamps, or unemployment insurance," he said. "They have other interests."

Talcove alleged some criminals use stolen funds to finance sex trafficking by bringing women from other countries and "renting them out" across the U.S., all while profiting from their "ill-gotten gains."
"What they have to look for is beyond the fraud that they found to see if they're involved in drugs, human trafficking, threats to our democracy, weapons," he said.

Calling the fraud a "national security issue," Talcove said some investigations have uncovered criminal groups involved in benefit fraud, including foreign cybercrime organizations such as APT41, a Chinese-linked hacking group.

"When you start looking at the criminal groups that are involved, APT41 and some of their peers and associates, as well as some of the other groups from North Korea and other countries, it is, right now, a national security issue," he said.
FBI LAUNCHES 'MOST WANTED FRAUDSTERS' LIST AS DOJ CHARGES OHIO DEFENDANTS IN $30M MEDICAID SCHEME FOR KIDS

Federal agents enter an office building as a search warrant is executed at Ultimate Home Health Services over potential Medicaid fraud, on Dec. 18, 2025, in Bloomington, Minnesota. (Christopher Juhn/Anadolu via Getty Images)
However, not all the money is sent to "overseas criminal organizations," according to Talcove.
"Now, some of it, granted, is being used for luxury goods, homes, cars, vacations, but a lot of it is just going right back to the transnational location that it came from," he said.
Talcove warned that unless investigators dig deeper, fraudsters will continue to exploit the system.
"They tend to get away with it because the investigation stops once you find the fraud," he said.
Turning to the government's role, Talcove said Democrats and Republicans must work together to tackle the nation's growing debt, starting with stronger efforts to combat fraud.

"My hope is the fiscal situation that we're currently in, driven by what's going on with the bond market, is going to force elected leaders at the state and federal level to start paying attention," he said.
