The stakes extend beyond diplomacy as disruptions from the war have disproportionately affected developing nations. India, the world's third-largest oil importer and consumer, has already suffered energy and inflation hits.

"The real measure of India’s success will therefore be its ability to keep BRICS sufficiently inclusive and functional to address Global South priorities while preventing geopolitical divisions from paralyzing the grouping," Pant said.
Kyra Colah works as a Writer and Associate Producer for Fox News.

title: Iran-backed terror group’s latest territorial grab threatens second global shipping chokepoint
summary: Iran-backed Houthi forces seized Yemen's Mocha port and advanced toward Bab el-Mandeb, threatening Red Sea shipping as Brent crude surged past $106.
story: Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin explains how attacks by Iran-backed Houthis in the Bab el-Mandab Strait could complicate U.S. military operations in the Middle East on ‘The Story.’

Iran-backed Houthi forces seized Yemen’s strategic port city of Mocha on Thursday and pushed toward positions overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, opening a potentially dangerous new front for global trade as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely constrained.

The advance threatens the southern gateway to the Red Sea just as Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on that route to bypass Hormuz — putting pressure on critical shipping lanes on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula and raising the risk of further disruptions to oil and commercial traffic through a key global trade choke point.

"Now you have Iran on one side of the Arabian Peninsula controlling Hormuz, and now the Houthis controlling Bab el-Mandeb on the other side of the peninsula," Hisham Al-Omeisy, senior Yemen advisor at the European Institute of Peace, told Fox News Digital. "Which basically is going to drive prices — oil prices, goods and everything else — up exponentially."
IRAN-BACKED TERROR PROXY HOUTHIS THREATEN FRESH ATTACKS AFTER YEMEN AIRPORT STRIKE

A vehicle burns after being attacked by Houthis during fighting with Saudi-backed forces at a location given as Al Jawf, Yemen, in this still image taken from a handout video released Sept. 9, 2026. (Al Masirah/Handout via Reuters)

On background, a senior administration official told Fox News Digital: "The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges. We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability."

Yemeni government sources said Thursay the Houthis captured Mocha and reached the Hanish Islands, while Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces withdrew south toward Dhubab, which sits directly on the Bab el-Mandeb opposite the strategic island of Perim. Control of Dhubab and Perim would be critical to gaining a stronger hold over the strait, Yemeni government sources told Reuters on Sept. 10.

Bab el-Mandeb is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point and connects the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea and, farther north, the Suez Canal. It is a major artery for goods moving between Asia and Europe as well as energy shipments.
Its importance has grown dramatically during the Iran conflict.
WHO CONTROLS THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ RIGHT NOW? HERE'S WHAT THE SHIP TRAFFIC ACTUALLY SHOWS

Members of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces react during what they say are clashes with Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis in a location given as near Al-Hazm, Yemen, in this screen grab obtained from a handout video released Sept. 9, 2026. (Media Centre Of The Yemeni Armed Forces/Handout via Reuters)

The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported Sept. 9 that crude oil and petroleum liquids moving through Bab el-Mandeb averaged 8.1 million barrels per day in the second quarter of 2026, up from 5.4 million barrels per day in the final quarter of 2025. At the same time, flows through Hormuz plunged from 21.6 million barrels per day to just 4.9 million. The EIA attributed the increase at Bab el-Mandeb in part to Saudi Arabia rerouting crude through its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu to avoid Hormuz.
Al-Omeisy said the danger extends beyond the Houthis’ geographical gains. He said retreating government forces left behind military materiel that could strengthen Houthi forces on other fronts.

"People are focused on taking Mocha and those outposts on the Red Sea," Al-Omeisy said. "But the military side is terrible, particularly the equipment, the munitions, the vehicles, the drones that were at those military camps, which they can now, in turn, use against the government forces elsewhere."
RUBIO ACCU.S.ES IRAN OF FLYING IRGC PERSONNEL INTO YEMEN AS HOUTHI THREAT ESCALATES

Members of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces fire a tank during what they say to be clashes with Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis in a location given as near Al-Hazm, Yemen, in this screen grab obtained from a handout video released Sept. 9, 2026. (Media Centre Of The Yemeni Armed Forces/Handout via Reuters)

Reuters separately reported Thursday that Iranian arms and direct guidance from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards helped the Houthi advance, citing Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources. Two Iranian sources told Reuters that Tehran had instructed the Houthis to intensify attacks on Saudi Arabia and promised additional funding, weapons and senior officers. Iran has publicly denied directing Houthi operations.

The seizure comes amid what conflict-monitoring organization ACLED described Sept. 9 as the most serious escalation between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed camp since hostilities resumed in mid-July.
ACLED recorded at least 276 fatalities between Sept. 3 and 7 as clashes spread across al-Dali, al-Bayda, Marib, Shabwa, al-Jawf, al-Hudayda and Taizz, according to an analysis published Sept. 9.

Sherwan Hindreen Ali, ACLED’s Middle East research manager, said fighting along the Red Sea coast had become particularly intense as both sides sought control over territory with direct strategic importance to Bab el-Mandeb.

"Fighting will remain focused on the fronts of the Red Sea coast in al-Hudaydah and Taizz, where both the Houthis and the Saudi Arabia/IRG have a vested interest in claiming the whole territory to deprive the other side of effective control of the strait of Bab el-Mandab," Ali said in an analysis.
Saudi Arabia itself has also become more deeply involved.
EXPERT WARNS OF 'GENERAL ESCALATION' OF FIGHTING IF HOUTHIS RESUME RED SEA CAMPAIGN

Houthi fighters gesture as they celebrate in front of the Security Directorate building in Hays, Yemen, in this screengrab taken from social media video released on Sept. 10, 2026. (Social Media/via Reuters)

Ali said Saudi forces launched at least 15 strikes against the Houthis between Sept. 3 and 7, mostly around Taizz, marking the highest number of Saudi strikes since Riyadh resumed military engagement against the Houthis in July.

The Houthis responded Sept. 8 with what Ali described as their largest wave of direct attacks on Saudi territory since March 2022, launching dozens of drones and ballistic missiles toward Abha, Jizan, Najran and Khamis Mushait. Ali said the attacks injured 73 people.
The widening fighting is now posing an early test for a new joint defense agreement between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey.
Al-Omeisy said the international response allowed the Houthis to exploit divisions among their opponents.

"The Houthis are also good in exploiting divisions and delays, they move rapidly on the ground to force a status quo while the international community debates merits, responsibilities and costs of an intervention."
The escalation also raises questions about Saudi Arabia’s newly signed defense agreement with Pakistan and Turkey.
IRAN-BACKED HOUTHI THREAT IN RED SEA COULD LEAD TO MAJOR US POLICY SHIFT, ANALYSTS SAY

A satellite image appears to show damage to the King Khalid Airbase at Saudi Airbase that Houthis claimed to have attacked on Sept. 8, in this handout picture obtained by Reuters on Sept. 9, 2026. The Saudi government’s media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. (2026 Planet Labs PBC/Handout via Reuters)

The agreement, signed last month in Mecca, states that an armed attack against one member will be considered an attack against all three, Reuters reported Sept. 10. But after Houthi drones and ballistic missiles struck Saudi cities and energy infrastructure this week, Pakistan said Thursday that no military response under the pact was currently being discussed.
"There is no such thing under discussion right now," Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said, according to Reuters. "When time comes [we] will act under the agreement."

The Houthis, meanwhile, have said international navigation through the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb remains safe, while maintaining that Saudi vessels are subject to their previously announced blockade, Reuters reported Thursday.
Al-Omeisy warned that reversing the Houthis’ latest territorial gains could become increasingly difficult.

"The Houthis are really good at capturing a position, they entrench really well," he said. "They send these massive reinforcements, and then it’s going to be extremely difficult to push them out of those areas."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

A satellite imagery shows Bab el Mandeb Strait, as Iran threatens using Yemen's Houthi allies to shut this gateway to the Red Sea, in this handout picture dated July 12, 2026. (Nasa Worldview/Handout via Reuters)

Oil markets were already responding to the widening regional threat Thursday. Brent crude jumped more than 5% to $106.60 a barrel by late Thursday morning, while U.S. crude climbed above $100 for the first time since May, according to Reuters.
Reuters contributed to the story.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Fire aboard cargo ship undergoing repairs at busy Chinese port leaves 25 people dead, five more injured
summary: A cargo ship called the Ocean Melody caught fire during repairs at Qingdao port, killing 25 of the 42 people on board the Liberian-flagged vessel.
story: The ship was docked at the port of Qingdao for repairs when a fire started, reportedly killing at least 25 people and injuring five others. (UGC via AP)
A cargo ship docked for repairs at a port on the northeastern coast of China caught fire Thursday, killing at least 25 people who were on board at the time, according to Chinese state media.

The ship was being fixed by Beihai Shipbuilding Co. in the port of Qingdao — one of the country's major shipping hubs — when it caught fire at approximately 11:15 a.m. local time, the Xinhua news agency reported.

A total of 42 people were on the vessel at the time of the blaze, and 12 of them were safely rescued, Xinhua reported. Five others were injured and taken to the hospital, where they are in stable condition.
CARGO SHIP ATTACKED BY SMALL CRAFT NEAR STRAIT OF HORMUZ, UK MARITIME AGENCY SAYS
In this photo released by Xinhua News Agency, a cargo ship is seen after it caught fire at a port in Qingdao, east China's Shandong Province, on Sept. 10, 2026. (Li Aoqiu/Xinhua via AP)
Photos released by Xinhua identified the ship as the Ocean Melody. The ship-tracking website VesselFinder lists it as sailing under the Liberian flag.
The Associated Press reported that the fire was extinguished at around 2:30 p.m., a little over three hours after it started. Videos online showed plumes of white smoke billowing from the ship.
The cause of the fire remains under investigation. Chinese authorities have not said what sparked the blaze while the vessel was undergoing repairs.
In this photo released by Xinhua News Agency, firefighters and crews gather near the cargo ship on fire on Sept. 10, 2026. (Li Aoqiu/Xinhua via AP)
TIM SHEEHY EXPOSES A 'SCARY' SHIPBUILDING COLLAPSE THAT LEAVES THE US VULNERABLE TO CHINA

China’s President Xi Jinping called for "intensified efforts" to provide support for those who were affected by the fire, Xinhua reported, adding that Premier Li Qiang said "trapped people" needed to be rescued.
Xi also called for ensuring "preventive measures are thoroughly implemented" and "resolutely prevent major and catastrophic accidents."
Aerial view of the illuminated Qingdao Qianwan Container Terminal at night on Sept. 6, 2026, in Qingdao, Shandong Province of China. (VCG/VCG via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Beihai Shipbuilding is a subsidiary of the state-owned China State Shipbuilding Corporation, the world's largest shipbuilder. According to the company's website, its primary businesses are shipbuilding and ship repair.

Qingdao, in China's Shandong province, is one of the country's busiest ports and a major center for shipbuilding, shipping and international trade. The port handles millions of containers each year and is home to several large shipyards.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: How 9/11 transformed synagogue security into a new reality for the Jewish community
summary: FBI data shows Jews face 63% of religiously motivated hate crimes as communities prepare for Rosh Hashanah on Friday, Sept. 11 amid rising threats.
story: Yeshiva University President Rabbi Ari Berman joins 'America's Newsroom' to discuss the rise of antisemitism in New York City following a hate crime attack at a Manhattan synagogue. Berman outlines campus security preparations prior to the start of classes as data shows 860 incidents in the city and nearly 1,200 statewide.

At sundown on Friday, Sept. 11, as America marks 25 years since the terrorist attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people, Jewish families across the country will welcome in Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish new year marking 5787.
They will enter synagogues at the moment of peak annual attendance, walking past armed guards, security cameras, secured doors and bag checks.
The convergence brings into focus how the Sept. 11 attacks transformed security in American synagogues and helped create the national infrastructure that now protects Jewish life.
FOX NEWS MEDIA ANNOUNCES EXTENSIVE 9/11 ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE FROM GROUND ZERO, PENTAGON AND SHANKSVILLE

An NYPD Mobile Command Unit stands outside of Temple Emanu-El on 65th Street near Central Park in New York City, May 22, 2025. This is part of an increase in security at Jewish organizations nationwide after an Israeli couple was killed in Washington, D.C. (Kevin C. Downs for Fox News Digital)

When Rosh Hashanah began six days after the attacks in 2001, a security guard stationed outside a synagogue was still unusual. Twenty-five years later, security is no longer an occasional precaution. It has become a permanent precondition of Jewish communal life.

"The confluence of events, the 25th anniversary of 9/11 and Rosh Hashanah, is really very meaningful to us," Eric Fingerhut, president and CEO of Jewish Federations of North America, told Fox News Digital. "If you trace the evolution of the security situation for the Jewish community in North America, you see that 9/11 really was a major turning point."

Before the attacks, Fingerhut said, synagogues may have relied on police to direct traffic during the High Holidays or installed basic alarm systems, but there was no widespread belief that Jewish communities needed protection from threats to their physical safety.
Law enforcement respond to a call at Temple Israel synagogue, Thursday, March 12, 2026, in West Bloomfield Township, Mich. (Corey Williams/AP Photo)

"That changed on 9/11," he said. "The Jewish community understood quite clearly that the people who attacked the World Trade Center and the Pentagon were attacking America that day, but they had a special animus for the Jewish community and the Jewish people."

Fingerhut said that shift led Jewish Federations of North America to help create the Secure Community Network after 9/11, giving communities a model for protecting Jewish institutions and a unified channel to federal law enforcement.

For generations, Rosh Hashanah preparation meant apples and honey, prayer books and the shofar. Now the checklist also includes secured entrances, emergency plans and congregants standing watch while their neighbors pray.
The price of that new reality is staggering.
MARYLAND SYNAGOGUE SUES COUNTY OVER LAW RESTRICTING CONCEALED CARRY NEAR HOUSES OF WORSHIP
Two flags flutter on a fence in front of Lower Manhattan and One World Trade Center at the Tear Drop 9/11 Memorial at sunset on June 13, 2026, in Bayonne, New Jersey. (Gary Hershorn/Getty Images)

A national study by Jewish Federations of North America found that Jewish communal institutions spend an estimated $1 billion annually on security. Based on an examination of more than 4,500 institutions, that amounts to nearly $2.8 million every day simply to keep Jewish life open and accessible.
The organization leads the national initiative placing professional security directors across all 141 Federation communities.
Rabbi Chaim Steinmetz, senior rabbi of Congregation Kehilath Jeshurun on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, described the contrast on his own block.

"If you walk past the churches on our block, the doors are wide open, inviting people in," Steinmetz told Fox News Digital. "But at our synagogue, there are security cameras, a double door system and a line of guards outside, at the cost of untold thousands of dollars."

That security is no longer reserved for major institutions or large cities. From New York and Florida to Michigan and Los Angeles, ordinary worshipers are training in situational awareness, access control, surveillance detection, emergency response and coordination with law enforcement.
A close-up image of a Jewish man wearing a traditional tallit (prayer shawl) and tefillin during morning prayers. (iStock)

The Community Security Service, or CSS, said more than 20,000 people completed its training in 2025. Of those, 6,100 volunteers protected 440 synagogues and nearly 100 Jewish events, logging more than 300,000 guard hours across 24 states.
The Secure Community Network (SCN) provides national intelligence and coordination. In 2025, it recorded 4,400 incident reports, trained 40,000 people and made 851 referrals to law enforcement.

"While the threat environment accelerates, our community has never been more prepared, informed or engaged," Michael Masters, SCN’s national director and CEO, told Fox News Digital. "This year our Duty Desk logged nearly 3,200 threat incidents, pacing ahead of last year."
Steinmetz said threats to the Jewish community "exploded after Oct. 7th," adding that "the hatred of Israel encourages antisemites to come out of the woodwork."

The FBI recorded 1,528 hate crime incidents targeting Jews in 2025, representing 63% of the nation’s 2,408 religiously motivated incidents. Jews comprise roughly 2% of the U.S. population, yet incidents targeting Jews represented 14% of all hate crimes reported nationwide.
ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE ESCALATES AS DEADLY WEAPON ATTACKS SURGE IN 2025: REPORT

Jewish students at El Camino Real Charter High School during a walkout protesting antisemitic incidents at the Woodland Hills school on Tuesday, Feb. 2024. (Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images)

During the first eight months of 2026, major crime fell 6.2% across New York City, while confirmed hate crimes targeting Jews rose 8%, from 212 to 229, according to new NYPD figures. That averages nearly one such crime every 25 hours.

Fox News Digital contacted NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch about the department’s High Holiday preparations. The NYPD said it will hold a briefing ahead of the holidays and provide additional security details at that time.

In neighboring New Jersey, the state Office of Homeland Security and Preparedness (NJOHSP) said it is coordinating with the state Attorney General’s Office, New Jersey State Police, the FBI’s Newark field office, local law enforcement and community partners.
"Together, we are protecting houses of worship, helping ensure every New Jerseyan can practice their faith without fear, and keeping New Jersey safe and secure," NJOHSP said.
The coordination follows recent attacks on Jewish institutions.

On Aug. 14, a man was charged with allegedly disrupting a Friday night service attended by approximately 375 people at Manhattan’s Central Synagogue, damaging ceremonial candlesticks and assaulting a congregant and security guard. The charges against include federal hate crimes and damaging religious property resulting in bodily injury.

Five months earlier, an attacker inspired by Hezbollah rammed a pickup truck carrying gasoline and fireworks through the doors of Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, Michigan, according to the FBI. Armed with a rifle and hundreds of rounds, he struck one security guard and exchanged gunfire with others.
Inside were 140 children at the synagogue’s early childhood center. Every child and staff member escaped without physical injury and the guard survived.
For Steven Ingber, CEO of the Jewish Federation of Detroit, the assault remains a powerful reminder of the need for vigilance as families prepare to gather.

Members of the New York Police Department patrol in front of a synagogue on Oct. 13, 2023 in the Williamsburg neighborhood in the borough of Brooklyn in New York City. Security has increased in New York City in the wake of the Hamas attack on Israel and after a former leader of Hamas called for Friday the 13th to be a global Jihad day. (Stephanie Keith/Getty Images)

"We take the security of our community with the utmost seriousness, and, of course, the assault on Temple Israel remains fresh in our minds," Ingber said. "We will enter the High Holidays vigilant and prepared. But we will also enter them with confidence and pride."

Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek in suburban Detroit, who also serves as president of the Michigan Board of Rabbis, said Jewish Michiganders are entering the new year "with a feeling of heaviness."

"From marking the 25th year since the terrorist attacks on 9/11 to marking six months since the terrorist attack on our community and especially our children, anxieties are heightened," Starr told Fox News Digital exclusively. "We enter with heaviness, but we are also filled with hope for a better tomorrow."
LOX & LOADED: JEWISH GUN GROUP PARTNERS WITH NRA AMID RISING ANTISEMITISM
"No family should have to weigh their safety against their faith," Fingerhut said.

Employing one full-time security guard costs an estimated $90,000 annually, according to Jewish Federations of North America. The organization is advocating for greater federal support through the bipartisan Jewish American Security Act, which would strengthen security assistance for at-risk nonprofit institutions.
For Jewish communities, the question is no longer whether security is necessary, but who will bear the growing cost of making worship possible.

A Bronx man was charged with multiple hate crimes after allegedly disrupting Shabbat services and attacking a congregant and security member at Central Synagogue in Manhattan, police said. (REUTERS/Eduardo Munoz)
SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER
Steinmetz called that cost "a vicious tax on the Jewish community," one "levied by the antisemites."
For Fingerhut, the purpose of security is not simply to prevent an attack. It is to ensure fear never determines whether a Jewish family participates in Jewish life.

"We do not want anyone to make the choice not to participate in Jewish life because they are afraid for their safety," Fingerhut said. "What we have learned is that the visible presence of security, and the real impact of that security, is what enables and encourages people to come out and participate in Jewish life."
Fingerhut’s message to Jewish communities in America and around the world was clear: do not retreat, but continue to "lean into Jewish life."
He said, "We will make sure that there is safety and security in place so that we can all feel confident in our involvement in Jewish life."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
That is the purpose, according to the experts, of every guard, camera and volunteer: not to turn a synagogue into a fortress, but to ensure that Jewish life continues inside.

Ariella Noveck is a journalist specializing in antisemitism and Middle East affairs, with extensive experience covering Jewish communities worldwide. She can be followed on X and Instagram @AriellaNoveck

title: Fed raises interest rates for first time since 2023, defying Trump as inflation mounts
summary: The Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised its benchmark interest rates for the first time since 2023, in a move aimed at slowing inflation.
story: The Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised its benchmark interest rates for the first time since 2023, in a move aimed at slowing inflation that picked up again last month.
The Fed’s hike of 0.25% brings the central bank’s flagship rate to between 3.75% and 4.00%.
The Fed’s policymakers unanimously supported the rate hike and signaled one more interest rate hike could come before the end of the year.
The Fed’s decision, which defied the president’s wishes for lower interest rates, comes in response to elevated inflation readings as the war with Iran drives up prices.

“Uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments,” the Federal Reserve’s statement read. “Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal.”
The hike could also be the start of a rate-hiking cycle. Historically, when a central bank raises rates once, it follows that up with additional increases.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Fed chairman Kevin Warsh said at a press conference in Washington following the announcement.
“We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed,” he said. “Today, the FOMC decided that this standard has not been satisfied.”
Released alongside the Fed’s rate decision today were economic projections. As of this week, all but two members of the Federal Open Market Committee forecast another rate increase later this year.

The rate hike comes despite years of demands by President Donald Trump for lower interest rates. In early February, Trump told NBC News that Warsh would not have gotten the nomination unless he wanted to lower rates.

“Warsh and the committee are sending a clear message that the Fed will not tolerate inflation drifting further above target, even in the face of political pressure from the White House,” said Brian Rehling, co-head of global fixed income at Wells Fargo.
Warsh was asked by a reporter Wednesday what his message for the president was be about the rate hike. “I’ve got nothing for you on a discussion with the president,” he replied.
But the war with Iran changed all of that, after the U.S. and Israel launched it Feb. 28. After less than four months on the job, Warsh is now presiding over a Fed that is increasing rates.

The Fed’s interest rate move comes after the Iran war sparked  a massive surge in the price of oil this year. This has, in turn, sent gas prices higher by more than 45% since the Iran war began in late February.
These energy prices have helped push inflation up to 3.4% as of August, above average U.S. wage growth of 3.1%.
But Warsh was clear on Wednesday about the limits of the Fed’s power to impact direct cots consumers pay.
“We cannot affect any individual price, whether it be oil prices, whether it be foodstuffs at the grocery store,” Warsh told reporters.
“But what we can do, and will do, is ensure that any change in relative prices don’t broaden out, don’t have second and third order effects in the economy.”
As Warsh spoke, major stock indexes reversed their earlier gains and turned lower for the trading session.

By the end of his remarks, the S&P 500 had fallen 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite was down 0.2%. The Dow fell almost 500 points, weighed down by sizable drops in shares of Boeing, IBM and American Express.
Following Wednesday’s rate increase, the 30-year Treasury bond yield declined slightly, but remains at its highest level in years. The critical 10-year Treasury bond yield was flat.
Warsh attributed the recent surge in bond yields to three factors.

“First is economic strength,” he said. The second was “the situation in hotspots around the world,” an apparent reference to the Iran war and war in Ukraine, both of which have restricted global energy supplies. The third factor, he said, was competition for capital from artificial intelligence companies.

title: House to leave early, punting Hegseth impeachment vote until after November elections
summary: House lawmakers will leave early for the November midterm elections after Republican leaders canceled votes for Thursday.
story: House lawmakers will leave Washington on Wednesday night for the last time before the November midterm elections, after GOP leaders said they were canceling votes set for Thursday.
The change in schedule means that the House won’t vote on Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky’s resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth until after Election Day.

GOP leaders insisted their decision had nothing to do with Massie’s impeachment efforts. But they were eager to avoid a difficult vote for many of their vulnerable Republican members who have been uneasy with Hegseth’s leadership during the unpopular six-month war with Iran.
Talking to reporters Wednesday, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., slammed the Massie impeachment effort as “ridiculous” and defended Hegseth.

“It’s a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention. It will immediately be tabled, of course. ... We’ll probably do it when we come back, but it’s a stunt,” Johnson said (tabling would effectively kill the measure). “Secretary Hegseth has done an extraordinary job, the Department of War. We’re in the middle of international conflicts right now, and we should not be playing games with national security.”

Massie filed his resolution to impeach Hegseth as “privileged” on Tuesday, meaning the House would need to act on it within two legislative days. That set up a vote no later than Thursday, but then GOP leaders scrapped votes that day, pushing the impeachment vote until after the election.
The House is slated to return to Washington on Nov. 9. Meanwhile, the Senate will remain in session for the next three weeks.
Johnson, who is fighting to preserve his razor-thin GOP majority, said he wanted his members to return home and get back on the campaign trail.

“It’s time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people, to go and explain all the great things we’ve done. You’ve seen the record. You’ve seen what we’ve delivered ... the largest middle- and working-class tax cut in U.S. history. We have the violent crime rate at a 126-year low,” Johnson said.

It’s “an extraordinary record of achievement,” he added, “and so I’m excited for my Republican colleagues to go home and talk to the American people, work in their districts, and explain to them not only serving their constituents but explaining to them all the great things we’ve done for them and all the things we’re going to do in the days ahead.”

Massie, who has served in Congress since 2012, has clashed repeatedly with House GOP leaders, President Donald Trump and Hegseth over the Iran war. The congressman voted for multiple Iran war powers resolutions to restrict Trump’s military operations in Iran and Venezuela.

Last year, Trump and his political team recruited former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein to run against Massie in the GOP primary in Kentucky. In an unusual move, Hegseth campaigned for Gallrein one day before the May primary election. Massie lost.
On Tuesday, with no advance warning, Massie took to the House floor and began reading his impeachment resolution.

Hegseth “has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution, if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law,” Massie said.

title: Supreme Court pushes back against Trump and GOP ahead of the midterm elections
summary: The Supreme Court’s recent rulings on mail-in ballots and redistricting foreshadow a frosty reception to further attempts to change the rules before the election, experts said.
story: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court in the last week has delivered major blows to President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans that suggest the justices will not be receptive to last-minute efforts to change election rules heading into the midterms.
With control of Congress at stake, the court on Monday night blocked Trump’s plan to exert federal control over mail-in ballots via a Postal Service regulation.
The decision came after the court twice last week ruled against Republicans by declining to revive a new congressional map in Missouri that would have eliminated one of two Democratic-held districts.

While the court has a 6-3 conservative majority that often rules for Republican priorities, there are limits to how receptive some justices are to more extreme requests, election law experts told NBC News. That’s especially true for cases that could disrupt voters when an election is close or already underway.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Justin Levitt, an NBC News contributor and election law expert at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, said the recent decisions show “there aren’t five votes for abject chaos.”

“I think the court is going to pay very close attention to any extraordinary actions that destabilize the electoral process,” said Bob Bauer, who served as White House counsel under President Barack Obama. “There’s a signal here that this sort of late intervention is going to receive scrutiny.”

On the left, the Supreme Court has been viewed with particular distrust and alarm as it relates to election issues following a major ruling in the spring that further weakened the landmark Voting Rights Act.
In the aftermath, the court quickly allowed Republican states to draw new congressional maps that eliminated majority-Black, Democratic-held seats.
But now it is Trump who appears angered and frustrated by the court’s actions.

“It is a big loss for Republicans, and America itself, and makes cheating by the Radical Left ‘Dumocrats,’ on Mail-In Ballots, a much easier thing to do — And now they have an open field to do so!” he said in a Truth Social post on Tuesday, repeating his unfounded claims about widespread election fraud.
With some states already sending out ballots for the midterm elections, timing was an issue for Republicans in both cases.

The Missouri Supreme Court faulted Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins for delaying a decision on whether the new map could be challenged, ultimately finding him in contempt for defying its ruling in favor of plaintiffs.
As for the Postal Service, it pushed through the new regulation despite concerns raised by election officials that they would be unable to implement it in time.

“In both instances, the court said we’re not going to countenance that,” said Travis Crum, an NBC News contributor and law professor at Washington University in St. Louis. “I do think that the Missouri case is going to send the message that dragging your feet like this is not going to be rewarded by the Supreme Court.”

As the November elections loom, efforts to make late changes to the rules, including any new proposals from the Trump administration relating to mail-in ballots, are likely to meet with a similarly frosty reception from the justices, experts said. They cautioned, though, that it is too early to say what new litigation could arise ahead of or after Election Day.

Among the concerns that have been raised by some election officials are that the Trump administration could post federal immigration agents near polling places, although officials have said they have no current plans to do so.

As he has done previously, Trump might also complain about mail-in ballots being counted after in-person votes, claiming voter fraud because the outcome might appear to change, even though it is customary for various jurisdictions to continue counting ballots after Election Day under state law.

States with competitive elections, especially those that could determine control of the Senate, could be a particular focus for any Election Day or post-election litigation. These include Texas and Georgia, two states under Republican control with competitive races. Alaska, where votes often take a long time to count, is another state that could attract litigation, with Democrats hoping to win the Senate race there.

One fear among election administrators is that the federal government could try to seize ballots and other voting records over claims of election fraud similar to those Trump and his allies raised, and courts rejected, following the 2020 presidential election. In January, the FBI searched an election office in Georgia, seizing 2020 election ballots.

But as the Supreme Court has shown in other cases, the conservative majority follows its own agenda, not Trump’s, and has delivered him major defeats this year on his sweeping tariffs and plan to roll back birthright citizenship.
“This court is radically conservative,” Levitt said, “but not actually in the tank for Trump’s particular version of personalist chaos.”

title: Apple’s record night and Colbert’s Emmys wins highlight TV in transition
summary: Apple took home a total of 28 trophies, with a record 14 for freshman comedy “Widow’s Bay.”
story: Maybe it was watching Stephen Colbert get his final two “Late Show” Emmys engraved at the after-party. Or hearing the rowdy Apple TV contingent in the audience whoop it up every time “Widow’s Bay” notched another win.
But inside the Peacock Theater on Monday night, this year’s Emmy Awards felt like a transition to a new era of television.
As the TV Academy’s events crew rolled away the blue carpet, the event gave us plenty of moments to remember. Here are just a few ...
A host with assists

With an opening musical number starring New York Knicks point guard Jalen Brunson and a “Law & Order: SVU” skit starring Taylor Swift, host Mariska Hargitay called in plenty of favors from her famous friends to help lend the Emmys a little star power. Hargitay, the show’s first female host in 15 years, rotated through at least 10 wardrobe changes, including a “Game of Thrones”-style fur cape and black power suit. But the uniform she kept on all night was cheerleader for the medium of television, going so far as to repurpose a line from Nicole Kidman’s viral AMC Theatres commercial to say, “At the end of the day, we come to TV for magic.”

title: Alex Ovechkin, all-time NHL goal scorer, appears in ad supporting Vladimir Putin
summary: Washington Capitals forward and NHL all-time leading goal scorer Alex Ovechkin appeared in an ad backing Russian President Vladimir Putin.
story: Washington Capitals forward and NHL all-time leading goal scorer Alex Ovechkin appeared in an ad backing Russian President Vladimir Putin, bringing renewed attention to the player’s controversial, longtime support for the authoritarian ruler.

The TV spot came to light just this week, showing Ovechkin standing in a group that included Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and retired Detroit Red Wings defenseman Viacheslav “Slava” Fetisov, professing their support of Putin’s United Russia party.
The Capitals confirmed that Ovechkin appeared in the spot and said the player’s off-the-ice political work will have no impact on the upcoming NHL season.

“Alex Ovechkin is a Russian citizen who lives in Moscow with his family during the offseason and will live there following his retirement,” team spokesman Sergey Kocharov said in a statement to NBC News on Wednesday.

“This summer, while in Russia, he was asked by his country to participate in a video campaign. As the longest-tenured athlete in Washington, D.C. and a pillar of the community, his focus and ours is on the season ahead and the continued impact he makes on the ice and in our city.”
Ovechkin has had a long, close relationship with Putin. Back in 2017, Ovechkin launched the “Putin Team” social movement.

Russia has been an international pariah since Putin  — who has run the country as president or prime minister since 2000 — launched the invasion of neighboring Ukraine in February 2022. Over 250,000 Russian soldiers, up to 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers and nearly 14,000 Ukrainian civilians are estimated to have been killed in the war.
Hall of Fame goaltender Dominik ‘The Dominator” Hašek has been particularly outspoken against the Putin regime and its supporters.
Hašek called Russia’s ongoing invasion “an imperialist war in Ukraine” and circled Ovechkin’s face in a picture of campaign supporters in an X posting this week.
“Because of each of them, many Ukrainians and Russians will be killed,” wrote Hašek, a native of Pardubice, Czech Republic, who played 16 seasons in the NHL, 9 with the Buffalo Sabres.
Ovechkin, who turns 41 this week, has tallied 929 goals in 21 NHL seasons, all with the Caps.
The three-time Hart Trophy winner  overtook Wayne Gretzky on the all-time goal scoring list when he found the back of the net during an April 6, 2025 game against the New York Islanders.
Ovechkin has hoisted the Stanley Cup once, leading Washington to the title in 2018. He also won the Conn Smythe Trophy that year, as playoff MVP.
The Caps open training camp on Thursday, ahead of the 2026-27 campaign. Washington’s regular season opener is set for Oct. 2 against the Stanley Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes.

title: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles says she’s cancer-free
summary: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles announced Wednesday that she is now cancer-free after being diagnosed with breast cancer in March.
story: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles announced Wednesday that she is now cancer-free after being diagnosed with breast cancer in March.
“After a medical appointment at the Mayo Clinic this week, my pathology results came back clear. I am cancer free,” she wrote in a post on X.

Wiles, 69, who has served as President Donald Trump’s White House chief of staff since the beginning of his second term, thanked him for his “unwavering support.” She added that she’s “deeply grateful and will continue to work to advance his America First Agenda.”
She first announced in mid-March that she had been diagnosed with breast cancer, which had been caught in the early stages, and that she’d received a “strong prognosis.”

According to the American Cancer Society, breast cancer is the most common cancer diagnosed among women in the U.S. and is the second-leading cause of death from cancer among women, with lung cancer being first.
It’s not clear what type of breast cancer Wiles had.
Trump had first disclosed Wiles’ diagnosis on Truth Social before she released an update about her health, saying that she would receive treatment.
At the time, the president added that Wiles would be “spending virtually full time at the White House, which makes me, as President, very happy!”

He added, “Her Strength and her Commitment to continue doing the job she loves, and does so well, while undergoing treatment, tells you everything you need to know about her. Susie, as one of my closest and most important advisors, is tough and deeply committed to serving the American People. She will soon be better than ever!”

title: House votes to hold Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt of Congress
summary: The House of Representatives voted unanimously Wednesday to find billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for refusing to comply with subpoenas related to a congressional probe into the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
story: The House of Representatives voted unanimously Wednesday to find billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for refusing to comply with subpoenas related to a congressional probe into the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Members passed the measure by unanimous consent one day after the House Oversight Committee voted 41-0 recommending the full House take action against Black for refusing to fully cooperate with its investigation into Epstein.

The resolution says “Mr. Black’s willful refusal to comply with the Oversight Committee’s subpoenas constitutes contempt of Congress and warrants referral to the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia for prosecution as prescribed by law.”

Attorneys for Black, co-founder and former head of the prestigious investment firm Apollo Global Management, released a statement calling the House measure an “outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr. Black.”

“The full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee’s actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman Comer,” they wrote.
Earlier this month, Black sued the Oversight Committee, seeking to block subpoenas it had issued for his appearance and nondisclosure agreements tied to Epstein.

Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., the committee chair, said Wednesday’s action shows that “No one is above the law. Leon Black defied two subpoenas, and the U.S. House of Representatives acted swiftly to find him in contempt of Congress.”

The top Democrat on the panel, Rep. Robert Garcia of California, called the vote “an important step towards justice and accountability.” He said members need to know why Black “gave Jeffrey Epstein $180 million dollars.”
Black had a lengthy business relationship with Epstein, a financier who died in jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.

Black announced he was stepping down as Apollo CEO in January 2021 after an internal review found he had paid Epstein $158 million between 2012 and 2017 for advice on tax and estate planning services. The review found that Black was not involved in Epstein’s criminal activities.

Black has said he didn’t engage in any wrongdoing and “deeply” regrets his involvement with Epstein, who died in jail in 2019 awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges. Black hasn’t been accused of wrongdoing by law enforcement, and he has denied any involvement in or awareness of Epstein’s illegal activity.

Black voluntarily sat for a closed-door transcribed interview with the Republican-led committee in late June, but it ended early with lawmakers slapping him with two subpoenas for allegedly not being forthcoming.
Attorneys for Black said the questioning went well beyond the parameters of the panel’s investigation and accused the lawmakers of engaging in a fishing expedition.
“This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr. Black,” one of the lawyers, Susan Estrich, said earlier this month.
He didn’t show up for a deposition the committee scheduled for Sept. 3 and filed suit against the panel.
In a statement Tuesday, Black’s attorneys called the contempt action “retaliation” for their client exercising his constitutional rights.

title: Fed raises interest rates for first time since 2023, defying Trump as inflation mounts
summary: The Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised its benchmark interest rates for the first time since 2023, in a move aimed at slowing inflation.
story: The Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised its benchmark interest rates for the first time since 2023, in a move aimed at slowing inflation that picked up again last month.
The Fed’s hike of 0.25% brings the central bank’s flagship rate to between 3.75% and 4.00%.
The Fed’s policymakers unanimously supported the rate hike and signaled one more interest rate hike could come before the end of the year.
The Fed’s decision, which defied the president’s wishes for lower interest rates, comes in response to elevated inflation readings as the war with Iran drives up prices.

“Uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments,” the Federal Reserve’s statement read. “Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal.”
The hike could also be the start of a rate-hiking cycle. Historically, when a central bank raises rates once, it follows that up with additional increases.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Fed chairman Kevin Warsh said at a press conference in Washington following the announcement.
“We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed,” he said. “Today, the FOMC decided that this standard has not been satisfied.”
Released alongside the Fed’s rate decision today were economic projections. As of this week, all but two members of the Federal Open Market Committee forecast another rate increase later this year.

The rate hike comes despite years of demands by President Donald Trump for lower interest rates. In early February, Trump told NBC News that Warsh would not have gotten the nomination unless he wanted to lower rates.

“Warsh and the committee are sending a clear message that the Fed will not tolerate inflation drifting further above target, even in the face of political pressure from the White House,” said Brian Rehling, co-head of global fixed income at Wells Fargo.
Warsh was asked by a reporter Wednesday what his message for the president was be about the rate hike. “I’ve got nothing for you on a discussion with the president,” he replied.
But the war with Iran changed all of that, after the U.S. and Israel launched it Feb. 28. After less than four months on the job, Warsh is now presiding over a Fed that is increasing rates.

The Fed’s interest rate move comes after the Iran war sparked  a massive surge in the price of oil this year. This has, in turn, sent gas prices higher by more than 45% since the Iran war began in late February.
These energy prices have helped push inflation up to 3.4% as of August, above average U.S. wage growth of 3.1%.
But Warsh was clear on Wednesday about the limits of the Fed’s power to impact direct cots consumers pay.
“We cannot affect any individual price, whether it be oil prices, whether it be foodstuffs at the grocery store,” Warsh told reporters.
“But what we can do, and will do, is ensure that any change in relative prices don’t broaden out, don’t have second and third order effects in the economy.”
As Warsh spoke, major stock indexes reversed their earlier gains and turned lower for the trading session.

By the end of his remarks, the S&P 500 had fallen 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite was down 0.2%. The Dow fell almost 500 points, weighed down by sizable drops in shares of Boeing, IBM and American Express.
Following Wednesday’s rate increase, the 30-year Treasury bond yield declined slightly, but remains at its highest level in years. The critical 10-year Treasury bond yield was flat.
Warsh attributed the recent surge in bond yields to three factors.

“First is economic strength,” he said. The second was “the situation in hotspots around the world,” an apparent reference to the Iran war and war in Ukraine, both of which have restricted global energy supplies. The third factor, he said, was competition for capital from artificial intelligence companies.

title: Attorneys in Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs’ $100M defamation suit seek to withdraw over unpaid fees
summary: Attorneys for Sean “Diddy” Combs’ are dropping the rapper and music executive as a client in his $100 million defamation lawsuit.
story: Attorneys for Sean “Diddy” Combs’ are dropping the rapper and music executive as a client in his $100 million defamation lawsuit.

Michael Tremonte, a partner at Sher Tremonte LLP, said Combs, 56, “has not paid a substantial balance of attorney’s fees, costs, and expenses,” according to a declaration to withdraw as counsel, filed Monday in the Southern District of New York.
Tremonte said in the filing that Combs is more than six months behind on fees, and that there has been “a total breakdown in cooperation and communication between Mr. Combs and the Firm.”
Combs has “declined to make himself available for timely, substantive, and direct communications about his cases for over four months,” the filing states.

“The Firm’s representation has been rendered unreasonably difficult by Mr. Combs’s lack of cooperation, resulting in a breakdown in attorney-client communications and rendering Sher Tremonte incapable of continuing to provide effective legal services to Mr. Combs,” the filing says.

Tremonte was defending Combs in civil litigation, including a $100 million defamation lawsuit against Courtney Burgess, Ariel Mitchell and Nexstar Media Inc.  He did not represent Combs in his criminal trial in New York City last year.
Through his spokesperson, Juda Engelmayer, Combs said the split was his decision.

“I made the decision to switch lawyers because I won’t let anyone take advantage of me by overcharging me and running up bills that were never approved,” he said. “This is strictly a business matter, and any talk about unpaid fees is just part of our dispute over those unapproved charges.”
Tremonte pushed back in an email, writing that his firm “represented Mr. Combs zealously and very efficiently under challenging circumstances.”

“As stated in our court filings, we are withdrawing from representing him because he has not paid his long-overdue invoices and has become uncooperative,” Tremonte said. “Any suggestion that we overcharged him is simply false.”
Combs is serving a 50-month sentence at a New Jersey federal prison on two interstate prostitution convictions stemming from that case. Prosecutors had sought 11 years.
He was acquitted of the more serious charges, including racketeering and sex trafficking and has maintained his innocence, pleading not guilty to all counts.
His release is scheduled for May 8, 2028, according to Federal Bureau of Prisons records, thought it could come sooner with  good behavior.
In July, Combs was moved to solitary confinement after a fight with another inmate, a source with knowledge of the matter told NBC News.

title: NBC Los Angeles helicopter crash shatters tight-knit local news community
summary: The television news helicopters that circle Los Angeles have been fixtures of the city’s sky for decades, symbols of a hard-driving but close-knit media market.
story: The television news helicopters that circle Los Angeles have been fixtures of the city’s sky for decades, symbols of a hard-driving but close-knit media market. The crews aboard the choppers cover police chases and FBI raids, Hollywood scandals and sports celebrations, earthquakes and wildfires.

The city’s TV news community was confronted with a tragedy of its own Tuesday when a helicopter used by the local NBC station crashed and burst into flames while hovering near the scene of a fatal bus collision. The chopper crash killed the two people aboard, journalist Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw, and one person on the ground. Two people died in the bus collision.

In wrenching on-air remarks and social media posts, Los Angeles news anchors and their colleagues attempted to process their grief while continuing to report on the accident. The outpouring illustrated the tight bonds linking colleagues who found themselves at the center of the story in the nation’s second-largest broadcasting center.

NBC Los Angeles’ Robert Kovacik, who joined the station 22 years ago, reported live from a commercial intersection in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in the San Fernando Valley. Microphone in hand, he stood just feet away from the Metro bus and the SUV that had collided when his crew’s cameras panned to plumes of black smoke rising behind a nearby 7-Eleven. He rushed to that scene.

Colleen Williams, a 40-year veteran of NBC Los Angeles and one of the city’s most recognizable broadcasting personalities, confirmed on air hours later that the station’s helicopter had gone down. Hands clasped, she spoke haltingly and seemed to fight back tears.

“We’ve been piecing it together here. We knew it was a news chopper, we knew we’d lost contact with our people out there, and we’ve just received the confirmation that, in fact, NewsChopper4 went down just before 7 o’clock tonight in Chatsworth,” Williams said to the camera. “We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, to process and to regroup.”

Kovacik sobbed and wiped away tears from inside a Los Angeles Police Department vehicle. He kneeled behind yellow police tape as elected officials, including Mayor Karen Bass, held an evening news conference about the accidents.
“This is a very, very, very tragic day in Los Angeles,” Bass said.

The news conference was short and solemn. Reporters from other outlets remained mostly silent, asking the mayor only one question. In tragic moments like these, Bass said, Los Angeles residents do what they do best — “come together.”

When the news conference concluded, Bass approached Kovacik and gave him a long hug. Political officials and first responders expressed their condolences to him; Kovacik thanked firefighters for arriving so quickly and doing everything they could to help Moreno and Marciniw.
The cause of the crash remained unknown Wednesday.

Jeff Wald, a former news director at rival local station KTLA, said Tuesday’s accidents were so devastating for the city partly because of the familial atmosphere inside the walls of its local newsrooms.

“What happens in this business is you wind up spending holidays, weekends, late nights and early mornings with these people, your colleagues. They become your second family,” he said in a phone interview. “Whenever I would hire somebody for these types of helicopter jobs, I worried about their safety.”
In a post on X, Frank Buckley, an anchor at KTLA, paid tribute to “our friends at NBCLA on a painful evening.”
“The helicopter pilots and crews at all of our stations are vital members of our teams who are dedicated to informing the public and this is a terrible loss,” he wrote.

Elex Michaelson, a CNN anchor who formerly co-hosted the evening news broadcast on KTTV, the local Fox affiliate, wrote on X that helicopters are “essential to covering the biggest stories in the vast news market of Southern California.” (In fact, news helicopters were pioneered in Los Angeles in the late 1950s.)

“I interned at NBC4 for years in college. Their team is filled with extraordinary people and great journalists,” Michaelson wrote in part. “My heart breaks for their team and the loved ones of everyone who lost their lives.”

Tuesday’s chopper accident took place 49 years after a Bell 206 news helicopter piloted by KNBC’s Francis Gary Powers, a former U.S. Air Force officer and CIA employee, crashed near the Encino neighborhood, killing him and cameraman George Spears. The two were returning from covering wildfire in Santa Barbara when their chopper lost fuel and came down.

Desmond Shaw, a helicopter news reporter for the CBS LA station, appeared Tuesday night from the seat of his chopper. He reflected on recent losses in his personal life, including the deaths of his parents, and said that anguish was “compounded” by news that the city itself had been struck by “a double tragedy.”
“The poor people that were caught in that bus crash today, I don’t want them to be forgotten either,” he said.
Shaw then invoked one of the core tenets of the news profession.
“We’re always saying, out of safety: cover the news, don’t be the news,” he said. “Unfortunately, gut-wrenchingly, they were part of the news tonight.”

title: Trump administration spent $9.5B last year on employee leave, driven by DOGE-era cuts
summary: The Trump administration spent $9.5 billion last year on paid administrative leave as it pushed to cut costs, the Government Accountability Office said.
story: The Trump administration spent an estimated $9.5 billion last year on paid administrative leave for federal workers as it pushed to cut costs by shrinking the government, according to a Government Accountability Office report released Tuesday.

Agencies’ use of paid administrative leave jumped by 435% from 2023 to 2025, the report found, and salary costs from such leave rose sixfold. That coincides with President Donald Trump’s decision in 2025 to create the Department of Government Efficiency led by tech billionaire Elon Musk, which enacted mass firings and dissolved the U.S. Agency for International Development.

Much of the increased leave cost — about $6.7 billion — came from  salary paid through a DOGE-era “deferred resignation program,” GAO found. Nearly 140,000 federal employees opted into the program, according to the Office of Personnel Management. It allowed for federal workers who agreed to quit in early 2025 to still be paid through September.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.

The GAO report emphasized that its numbers were estimates, noting that OPM “does not know the actual costs of the paid administrative leave used for workforce reduction efforts, including the deferred resignation program.”

“To calculate long-term savings, OPM needs to know short-term costs of paid administrative leave used for these efforts,” the report explained. “However, OPM cannot easily and accurately do this because the paid administrative leave used for workforce reduction efforts is reported with other types of general paid administrative leave.”

The deferred resignation program was unveiled just days into Trump’s second term, and federal workers received a “Fork in the Road” email laying out their options. Musk, who had quickly risen to the highest echelons of power in the administration, had previously sent an email with the same subject line to X employees, where he reshaped the company’s workforce.

At the time of the program’s announcement, then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said that if federal workers “don’t want to work in the office and contribute to making America great again, then they are free to choose a different line of work, and the Trump Administration will provide a very generous payout of 8 months.”

During Trump’s second term, the federal workforce has lost more than 271,000 employees as of July, according to data published by OPM. The figure includes voluntary and involuntary departures. The data indicates that between 2015, the earliest year provided, and 2025, when Trump took office again, the federal workforce grew every year.

title: Merriam-Webster gives its dictionary a ‘glow-up’ with 1,400 new words and definitions
summary: Merriam-Webster is giving its dictionary another “glow-up,” adding 1,400 words and definitions.
story: Merriam-Webster is giving its dictionary another “glow-up,” adding 1,400 words and definitions.
The dictionary publisher announced the additions on its website Tuesday. The new words and definitions include “shapewear,” “looksmaxxing” and “meme coin.”
“The new entries reflect words and meanings that have demonstrated widespread use over time, offering a window into the world today,” it said in the release.
Other words and definitions that made it into the dictionary include “parasocial,” “compute,” “vibe coding” and “superfood” (food rich in nutrients, including salmon, broccoli and blueberries).

As temperatures drop across the country, Merriam-Webster fittingly added “cuffing season” to its dictionary. The company defines the term as “a time of the year when people who are not married or in a relationship begin looking for a short-term romantic partner to spend the colder months of the year with.”

And amid widespread fears in recent days about AI’s impact on humanity, the company added “uncanny valley” to its collection of definitions. Merriam-Webster defines the term as “that creepy feeling that results from something artificial appearing almost—but not quite—human.”
The nod to AI follows Merriam-Webster’s word of 2025, “slop,” which it defines as “digital content of low quality that is produced usually in quantity by means of artificial intelligence.”
Merriam-Webster has not yet announced a Word of the Year for 2026. The company typically makes the announcement in the final quarter of the year.
The company said on its website that it adds new words and phrases to its repertoire based on frequent, widespread and meaningful use.

“The definer must judge whether there is enough evidence to put a new word in; that judgment will be reviewed by more senior colleagues as the dictionary moves through the editorial process, but there’s no committee, no advocacy, no meetings for new word inclusion,” the company said.

title: How Kraft Heinz is keeping its legacy brands affordable to cost-conscious shoppers
summary: For Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane, changes in the grocery marketplace demand a shift in strategy.
story: Years of high inflation have strained household budgets across America, putting a spotlight on the rising costs of necessities such as gas and groceries. They have also contributed to a shift in how consumers perceive value at the supermarket.
New research from McKinsey finds that Americans are increasingly turning away from name-brand foods to lower priced, private-label or store-brand products.
For Kraft Heinz CEO Steve Cahillane, these changes in the marketplace demand a shift in strategy.
“We can’t just rely on having a strong brand and saying that’s going to be enough,” he said in an interview on a tomato farm in Woodland, California, part of NBC’s “Business in America” initiative.
“Consumers have only so many dollars available for their food budget in a month’s time, and so you have to earn the right to be in that basket each and every day.”
In recent years, store brands have shed their traditional associations with lower quality ingredients and temporarily “trading down.”
Today, 85% of consumers believe private-label grocery products are just as good or better than those from name brands, McKinsey reports.

Kraft Heinz sells more than 200 brands, many of them household names such as Heinz ketchup, Kraft Mac & Cheese, Oscar Mayer meats, Capri Sun drinks, Miracle Whip spread, Velveeta, Philadelphia cream cheese and Kool-Aid.
But this is a challenging time to be in the name-brand food business. Last year, Kraft Heinz’s net sales in North America were down about 5% from 2024.
When Cahillane took the helm as CEO in January, he was tasked with turning the business around.
One part of that strategy, he said, is deploying promotional discounts more strategically.

“We’re working with our retail partners to make sure that at the beginning of the month, when consumers are really doing their big shops, that we’re out there with good offers across the board,” he said.
Consumers in general tend to have more spending power at the beginning of the month when government benefits such as SNAP are distributed, paychecks arrive and monthly budgets reset.
“Promotions can be an effective means by which to drive that initial purchase,” said Erin Lash, a senior director of consumer equity research at Morningstar.
But promotions can also create a new challenge: getting shoppers to come back once the deal is gone.
“Promotions can be kind of a slippery slope,” said Mark Mayer, associate professor of Marketing at Indiana University and a former Kraft Foods brand manager.
If customers “only buy your product when they can get it for a deal,” then the promotion defeats its purpose, he said.
Unlike store brands, a company like Kraft Heinz needs a pricing strategy that both appeals to shoppers and also protects the brand’s status.
“In general, competing on price is not great for established brands,” said Alexander Chernev, professor of marketing at the Kellogg School at Northwestern University.

Unless a company is specifically positioned from the outset as a discount brand, slashing prices can undermine a brand’s identity. This is especially true for legacy products like those in Kraft Heinz’s portfolio.
It requires Kraft Heinz to pull off a difficult balancing act: Making its products more affordable without diminishing the value of its brands.
Cahillane said that when it comes to pricing, Kraft Heinz is not lowering list prices across the board. Only where the economics make sense.
“The biggest price drop, where we’re bringing prices down, is most certainly in our coffee business,” which is home to brands like Maxwell House and Gevalia.
A drop in global coffee prices strengthens the economic case for price cuts. As of Wednesday, benchmark coffee futures were down 30% from a year ago.
Kraft Heinz is also offering some of their products in smaller sizes.

“This isn’t shrinkflation,” Cahillane said, “this is recognizing that if we’re selling a 32-ounce bottle of ketchup and that’s too much for a family… we have a smaller 8-ounce bottle at a very affordable price.”
It’s a strategy that has also been utilized by other major packaged food companies, including PepsiCo, Campbells and Mondelez, as they look to offer shoppers lower-priced options.
Ultimately, Kraft Heinz must give shoppers a reason to pay full price, Cahillane said. And quality is what will justify the premium.

“Value is affordability, but it’s also delivering the product quality and the promise that you’re making to consumers,” he said. “If they buy your brand, they’ll be receiving a value that they’re willing to pay for.”

title: U.S. accuses Russia of plot to kill a prominent dissident in Washington
summary: The Kremlin orchestrated a murder-for-hire plot against a prominent Russian dissident in Washington, D.C., this summer, the Department of Justice has said, as it unsealed charges against five people it alleged were part of a “global assassination network” aimed at causing “destruction and mayhem around the world.”
story: The Kremlin orchestrated a murder-for-hire plot against a prominent Russian dissident in Washington, D.C., this summer, the Department of Justice has said, as it unsealed charges against five people it alleged were part of a “global assassination network” aimed at causing “destruction and mayhem around the world.”

The five people charged are still at large, the DOJ said in the indictment unsealed late Tuesday, describing the wider operation being run by Russian intelligence as “brazen, aggressive, and far-reaching.”
The FBI said it had disrupted the plot, although officials did not detail how.

Since at least 2024, the network is alleged to have paid Americans and foreigners to spy on targets, “carry out targeted killings,” and “commit acts of terrorism against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries that are aligned, or perceived to be aligned, with Ukraine,” the DOJ said.

Asked for a response to the allegations by NBC News, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a daily briefing call with reporters that “until we have heard or seen any reasonable evidence and arguments based on at least something tangible, we do not consider it necessary to comment on this news.”
Russia has for decades been accused by Western governments of carrying out attempted and successful killings abroad. Despite substantial evidence, it has always denied these allegations.

The indictment did not name the intended victim in Washington. The DOJ lists the defendants as Yuri Khrameev, known as “Colonel Yuri,” 63, and his son Kirill Khrameev, 27, both of Russia; Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, known as “Viking,” both 35 and Cuban nationals; and Angel Eduardo Castro, 22, of Venezuela.
The indictment describes Durruthy as “an influential member of the Cuban diaspora living in Russia,” where it says Suarez and Castro also reside.
All face a conspiracy to finance terrorism charge. Yuri Khrameev, Suarez and Castro face an additional charge of conspiracy to commit murder for hire.
Yuri Khrameev is alleged to be a former Russian intelligence colonel, while his son is an officer in Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB.

Prosecutors allege the network recruited a Venezuelan citizen living in Brooklyn this summer, promising him between $1,000 and $1,500 to photograph and film two locations associated with the Washington target.

The man carried out the surveillance but declined an offer from Suarez and Castro of $40,000 to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target himself, prosecutors said. The alleged recruiters asked whether he knew somebody who would.
Suarez also offered substantial sums of money to other people in the U.S. to finish the job, the indictment said.

Messages quoted in the indictment show the conspirators allegedly referring to murder as “construction.” Surveillance instructions included putting the man’s phone into airplane mode and filming while passing the house.
Suarez allegedly said he also had people in Mexico who could carry out the killing, but they were delayed.
A second alleged plot involved a dissident believed to be living in Lithuania who the network accused of making derogatory statements about Russia.

In that case, a U.S. citizen was promised $200 to photograph the target’s address in 2025, then offered around $25,000 to kill him, prosecutors said. When he refused, Yuri Khrameev allegedly offered a “simpler job” — setting fire to a warehouse or attacking an electricity substation.
The purpose, Khrameev allegedly said, was to target “all the countries that are helping Ukraine.”
Durruthy, meanwhile, is accused of coordinating logistics for attacks in Prague in June 2024 and Lithuania that September.
Lithuanian authorities had publicly named Durruthy as wanted in January in a case involving attempts to burn military equipment intended for Ukraine, according to Lithuanian broadcaster LRT.

“These defendants allegedly operated as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit U.S. citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg.
“Actions like these represent a gross violation of our sovereignty and a threat to our national security.”
James C. Barnacle Jr., head of New York’s FBI office, said the agency “disrupted this operation through relentless work and rock-solid partnership.”

title: Is running in the cold dangerous? Experts weigh in
summary: Running experts give tips on how to stay warm while running in cold temperatures and suggest gear that will help you stay comfortable and warm.
story: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends on our timelines, like whether honey is good for your skin.

Frigid temperatures, icy roads and darker mornings can make running in the cold weather feel  a lot more challenging. But running outside during any time of year has its benefits. The fresh air is nice, and the scenery is more engaging than being on a treadmill at the gym.

“Running in the cold can be invigorating,” says Jay Silva, a Road Runners Club of America certified running coach with TeachMe.To, a site that helps you find coaches. “You just have to be smart about it and be prepared.”

So, how can you prepare yourself to run in cold weather so you can still enjoy the benefits of exercising outside? The key is to take a few preventative steps to keep yourself safe and ensure you have the right gear. With that in mind, I consulted running experts to get all the intel you need for running in the cold and also how to know when it’s just too cold to go for a run.

How to stay safe while running in the cold

Running in cold weather can be safe — up to a certain point. Experts I spoke to agreed that running outdoors when it’s lower than 15 degrees Fahrenheit or the windchill is below 10 degrees Fahrenheit is not advised. If you take the right precautions, anything above those temperatures can be safe to run in. Here’s what they suggest to prepare:

Spend time stretching: “It’s crucial to warm up indoors to get your muscles activated and ready,” says Taylor Wilson, a certified personal trainer in California. “Cold muscles are more prone to strain, so stretching can reduce risk of injury.” He suggests dynamic stretches like leg swings or lunges. Stay hydrated: When it’s hot and you’re sweating, it’s easy to remember to drink water. But staying hydrated is just as important in the colder weather. “Even though you sweat less, dehydration can creep up without you noticing it,” says Andrew White, a certified personal trainer and founder of Garage Gym Pro, a site that helps people set up home gyms. “Be mindful of drinking water before and after you run.” Watch for black ice: Black ice tends to pop up during the winter months. Pair that with the fact that the sun rises later and sets earlier and it can be easy to miss slippery patches on the road. “I can’t count the number of times I’ve been caught off guard by hidden ice patches, especially early in the morning,” says Silva. “Adjust your stride to be shorter and quicker to maintain better balance and avoid slipping.”Dress appropriately: Figuring out what to wear when running in cold weather can be tricky. While it’s tempting to bundle up so you’re warm as soon as you step outside, that may be the wrong move. You want to dress as if it is 10 to 20 degrees warmer than it actually is outside — you may be slightly cold when you first get outside, but you’ll warm up fast, says Silva. The other thing to consider is covering your hands, feet and head properly — three areas that tend to get particularly cold. Below, I’ve outlined exactly how to dress for running in colder weather and rounded up the best gear for it.
